The *Arthaviniścaya-sūtra*.
Homage to the Buddha!

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Eastern Park, in the mansion built by the bricklayer Sudatta, together with a great saṅgha of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks.

And there, with a voice like the drum of joy—deep, pleasant, and sublime—the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, I shall teach you the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; I shall proclaim the holy life that is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, pure, and pristine—namely, the discourse on the Dharma called *Arthaviniścaya*."
"Listen to that, and having heard it, attend to it; I shall speak.
"Very well, Blessed One," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke as follows:
And what, monks, is this Dharma discourse called the "Ascertainment of Meaning"? [It is:
(19) the factors of enlightenment, (20) the mindfulness of the limbs of enlightenment, (21) the four noble truths, and (22) the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

(23) the four grounds of self-confidence, (24) the four analytical knowledges, (25) the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, (26) the thirty-two marks of a great man, and (27) the eighty minor marks. This is the summary of the Dharma discourse on non-determination; herein one trains.
(1) There are five aggregates.
In this regard, monks, what are the five aggregates?
Namely: (1) the aggregate of form, (2) the aggregate of feeling, (3) the aggregate of perception, (4) the aggregate of mental formations—

The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness— these, monks, are the five aggregates. (2) The five aggregates of clinging.
In this regard, monks, what are the five aggregates of clinging?

They are as follows: (1) the aggregate of clinging to form, (2) the aggregate of clinging to feeling, (3) the aggregate of clinging to perception, (4) the aggregate of clinging to mental formations, and (5) the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
Monks, these are the five aggregates of clinging.
(3) There are eighteen elements.
In this regard, a disciple asks: what are the eighteen elements?

They are as follows: (1) the eye element, (2) the form element, (3) the eye-consciousness element; (4) the ear element, (5) the sound element, (6) the ear-consciousness element; (7) the nose element, (8) the odor element, (9) the nose-consciousness element; (10) the tongue element, (11) the taste element, (12) the tongue-consciousness element; (13) the body element, (14) the tangible object element, (15) the body-consciousness element; (16) the mind element, (17) the mental-object element, (18) the mind-consciousness element.
These eighteen elements are called the disciples.
(4) Regarding the twelve bases, the disciple asks: what are the twelve bases?

They are as follows: (1) the internal sense-base of the eye, (2) the external sense-base of form, (3) the internal sense-base of the ear, (4) the external sense-base of sound, (5) the internal sense-base of the nose, (6) the external sense-base of odor, (7) the internal sense-base of the tongue, (8) the external sense-base of taste, (9) the internal sense-base of the body, (10) the external sense-base of tangibles, (11) the internal sense-base of the mind, and (12) the external sense-base of mental phenomena.
These, O disciples, are called the twelve sense-bases.

(5) The twelvefold dependent origination. In this regard, monks, what is the twelvefold dependent origination? It is as follows: when ignorance exists, this comes to be; from the condition of ignorance, this arises.

Namely: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being. Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.

From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; and from the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
In that regard, what is ignorance? It is as follows: ignorance regarding the past, ignorance regarding the future, and ignorance regarding the present.
Knowledge regarding the internal, knowledge regarding the external,
and knowledge regarding both the internal and the external.
Knowledge regarding action,
knowledge regarding its ripening, and knowledge regarding the ripening of action.
Knowledge of the past limit, knowledge of the future limit, and knowledge of both the past and future limits.
Ignorance regarding the cause, knowledge regarding the fruit, and knowledge regarding both cause and fruit.
Knowledge regarding phenomena arisen from causes, knowledge regarding dependent origination,
and ignorance regarding dependently originated phenomena.
Knowledge of the Buddha, knowledge of the Dharma, and knowledge of the Saṅgha.
Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of its origin, and knowledge of its cessation.
Ignorance regarding the path, ignorance regarding wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, and ignorance regarding blameworthy and blameless phenomena.
Ignorance regarding those phenomena that should be cultivated and those that should not be cultivated;
ignorance regarding inferior and superior phenomena, and regarding dark and bright phenomena;
or, in brief, this [is ignorance] in every respect.
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) regarding things as they have been heard, which consists of non-ascertainment and false cognition, is subsumed under the category of *avidyā*.
This is what is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*). It is said that "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*).
What are the formations? There are three formations: bodily formation, vocal formation, and mental formation.
What is bodily formation? Inhalation and exhalation.
The phenomenon of bodily exertion is dependent on the body, based on the body, bound to the body, and exists relying upon the body.
Therefore, inhalation and exhalation are called bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*).
[Next is] vocal formation (*vāksaṃskāra*).
What is it? It is that which speaks what is to be said after deliberating upon its perishable nature, and not that which speaks without deliberation upon its perishable nature.
Therefore, it is called the vocal formation (*vāk-saṃskāra*) as something subject to destruction.
What is the mental formation (*manah-saṃskāra*)? It is both volition (*cetanā*) that is independent and volition that is deluded.
It is a mental factor that is wholesome, has the mind as its cause, is bound to the mind, and proceeds depending upon the mind.
Therefore, volition is called a mental formation (*manaḥ-saṃskāra*).
These, venerable sirs, are called the three formations.
"Consciousness has formations as its condition.
What is consciousness? It is the six groups of consciousness.
Which are the six? Namely: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, [body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness].
Body-consciousness and mind-consciousness—
these six groups of consciousness are called "consciousness.
With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises].
In that regard, what is name? It is the four formless aggregates.

Which four? The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness—this is name. What is form? Whatever is form—that is, the great elements beginning with the eye, etc.

And [it arises] depending on the four great elements. Which four? Namely: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element. What is the earth element? That which is heaviness and hardness. What is the water element? That which is fluidity and cohesion. The fire element...

What is it? It is that which possesses heat and the quality of maturation. What is the wind element (*vāyudhātu*)? It is that which possesses non-solidity, lightness, and mobility. When this form (*rūpa*) and the aforementioned name (*nāma*) are both condensed together as one, it is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).

"The five sense bases consist of name-and-form. What are the five sense bases? They are the sense bases of the five aggregates. Namely: the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.
Thus it is called the five bases.
Regarding the six bases, there are the sense-faculties and contact (*sparśa*).
What is contact? It consists of the six groups of contact.
Six: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.
Contact is liberated [from its object].
From the group of contacts arises feeling. What is feeling? It is the six groups of feeling.
Feeling born of contact—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Feeling born of contact with the tongue, body, and mind—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
This is called feeling.
From the group of feelings comes craving (*tṛṣṇā*). What is craving? It consists of the six groups of craving. Which six?
Craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena (*dharma*).
From the group of cravings comes grasping (*upādāna*). What is grasping? It consists of the four types of grasping.

Which four? They are: clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmopādāna*), clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*), clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*), and clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*). Regarding the statement "mantra consists of clinging": what is a mantra? There are three types of mantras.
Which three?
Namely: existence in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu), existence in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), and existence in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Among these, what is existence in the realm of desire?
Namely: the hot hells are below.
Which ones are below?
Namely: Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci.
The cold hells are below.
Which ones are below?
They are as follows: Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma.
Hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm.
Which six?
The gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods. [12]

In that regard, what is the continuity of form (*rūpa-saṃdhi*)? It is as follows: the Navakāyikas, the Navapurohitas, those belonging to the assembly of Mahābrahmā, the Apramāṇābhas, the Ābhāsvaras, the Parīttaśubhas, the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Anabhrakas, the Puṇyaprasavas, the Bṛhatphalas, the Abṛhas, the Atapas, the Sudṛśas, the Sudarśanas, and the Akaniṣṭhas.

What is that which consists of sound? It is as follows: "the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; also, the twenty-fourfold distinction of the objects of the formless deities. "In dependence upon the Dharma, that which consists of sound is impure. These are the three consistencies.

And craving has existence as its condition. What is birth? It is the actuality of those various classes of phenomena, the unsurpassed category of sentient beings: birth (*jāti*), being born (*saṃjāti*), arising (*upapatti*), descent [into the womb] (*avakrānti*), manifestation (*abhinirvṛtti*), appearance (*prādurbhāva*);
the projection of form; the projection of the elements (*dhātu*); the projection of the sense-bases (*āyatana*); the manifestation of the various forms;
the conjunction with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); and the aggregation of the atoms of the body.

Thus is birth described. "The sixfold decay is called aging. What is aging? It is that which is infirmity, decrepitude, wrinkled and furrowed skin, being worn out, graying of hair, becoming bent like a roof-rafter, and labored, rattling inhalation and exhalation.
Deceitfulness, the body being marred by freckles and moles, leaning on a staff, the body slumping forward,
the maturation and decline of the sense faculties; the state of the conditioned factors becoming ancient and worn out, their density, their dullness, their loss, and their decrepitude.
Thus is aging described.
What is death? It is the falling away of those beings from their respective classes of beings;

passing away, dissolution, destruction, death, the completion of time, the exhaustion of the lifespan, the exhaustion of heat, the cessation of the life-faculty, and the cessation of the aggregates of form.
This is called death.
When this death and the previously mentioned aging are both condensed together into one, it is called "aging-and-death.
This is the twelfth [link] of the twelvefold dependent origination.
(6) The Four Noble Truths. In this regard, monks, what are the four noble truths?

They are as follows: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

(1) In that regard, what is the noble truth of suffering? It is as follows: birth is suffering; aging is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; separation from the beloved is suffering; association with the unbeloved is suffering; not obtaining what one desires is also suffering; in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
This is called the noble truth of suffering.
(2) What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is as follows: craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there.
This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

(3) What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless abandonment, relinquishing, and forsaking of this very craving—which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there.
Cessation, disappearance, destruction, detachment, stopping, pacification, and vanishing—this is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
(4) In that regard, what is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering? It is precisely this right eightfold [path].
The Noble Eightfold Path; namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
This is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Thus it is understood more clearly.
Monks, these are the four noble truths.
(7) There are twenty-two faculties;
therein, monks, what are the twenty-two faculties?

Namely: (1) the eye faculty, (2) the ear faculty, (3) the nose faculty, (4) the tongue faculty, (5) the body faculty, (6) the mind faculty, (7) the female faculty, (8) the male faculty, (9) the life faculty, (10) the faculty of pain, (11) the faculty of mental distress, (12) the faculty of pleasure, (13) the faculty of mental joy, (14) the faculty of equanimity, (15) the faculty of faith, (16) the faculty of energy, (17) the faculty of mindfulness, (18) the faculty of concentration, (19) the faculty of wisdom, (20) the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," (21) the faculty of knowing, and (22) the faculty of one who has known.
Monks, these are the twenty-two faculties.
[17] The four meditative absorptions (dhyānas).
The four meditative absorptions.
In this regard, monks, what are the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)?

(1) Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first *dhyāna*, which is accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

(2) With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second *dhyāna*, which is free from applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of concentration.

(3) Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna, which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous.

(4) With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the previous disappearance of mental joy and dejection, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
These, monks, are the four dhyānas. [16]
(9) There are four attainments of the oblation; herein, the disciple asks: "What are the four attainments of the oblation?

(1) Here, the disciple, having reached the culmination, through the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space.
(2) Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness.
(3) Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever," he dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness.
(4) Having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, he dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These are called the four meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that are like disciples.
(10) There are the four divine abodes (*brāhmavihāra*). Among them, what are the four divine abodes that are like disciples? [16]

With a mind imbued with loving-kindness—unfailing, perfected, energetic, vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having pervaded one direction, suffused it, and attained it.

Likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, and across, everywhere, in every way, throughout the entire world, he dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, well-cultivated, free from enmity, free from ill will, and full of resolve. Having suffused it, he attains it and abides therein.

Thus, with a mind accompanied by (1) compassion, (2) sympathetic joy, and (3) equanimity—a mind that is unafflicted, perfected in exertion, vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having pervaded one direction, having suffused it, and having attained it.
These, monks, are the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras).
There are also four modes of practice (pratipadas).
In that regard, what are the four modes of practice?

(1) There is, monks, a painful mode of practice with sluggish direct knowledge; (2) there is, monks, a painful mode of practice with swift direct knowledge; (3) there is, monks, a pleasant mode of practice with sluggish direct knowledge; (4) there is, monks, a pleasant mode of practice with swift direct knowledge.
(1) In that regard, what is the painful mode of practice with sluggish direct knowledge?
In this case, a certain person is by nature intensely passionate, intensely hateful, and intensely deluded.

Due to his intense passion, he experiences the suffering and mental distress born of passion; due to his intense hatred, he experiences the suffering and mental distress born of hatred; and due to his intense delusion, he experiences the suffering and mental distress born of delusion.
For him, these five supramundane faculties become blessed, provided they are directed toward the goal, swift in their operation, and lead to the destruction of the outflows.
What are the five? Namely:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of awakening, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

He touches the joy of loving-kindness (*maitrānanda*) toward phenomena, which consists of the arising, increase, and dwelling of the five supramundane faculties—that is, for the sake of exhausting the unfavorable conditions. This is the difficult practice with slow fruition. (2) In that regard, what is the difficult practice with quick fruition?
In this case, a certain person is by nature intensely passionate, intensely hateful, and intensely deluded.

Because of his intense passion, he experiences from time to time the suffering and mental distress born of passion; because of his intense hatred, he experiences from time to time the suffering and mental distress born of hatred; and because of his intense delusion, he experiences from time to time the suffering and mental distress born of delusion.
For such a person, these five supramundane faculties are superior, sharp, and swift-acting.
Which five? Namely:

the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. Because these five supramundane faculties are complete, being characterized by direct knowledge, sharpness, and swift operation, he touches the concentration that pierces quickly and leads to the goal, namely for the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*).
This is the painful practice with direct knowledge.
(3) In that regard, what is the pleasant practice with swift superknowledge?

In this case, a certain person is by nature one who has little passion (*alparāga*), little suffering (*alpaduḥkha*), and little delusion (*alpamoha*). Because he has little passion, he does not frequently experience the pain and mental distress born of passion; because he has little aversion (*alpadveṣa*), he does not frequently experience the pain and mental distress born of aversion; and because he has little delusion, he does not frequently experience the pain and mental distress born of delusion. For him, these five supramundane faculties (*indriya*) are feeble, soft, not sharp, and not swift-moving. What are the five? Namely, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). Due to the feebleness, lack of sharpness, softness, and lack of swiftness of these five supramundane faculties, he touches a concentration that is feeble in its penetration and slow in its realization—namely, for the sake of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).
This is called the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge.

(4) In this regard, what is the pleasant practice for the sake of knowledge and supernormal powers? Here, a certain person is by nature one who has little passion, little suffering, and little delusion. Because he has little passion, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of passion; because he has little hatred, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of hatred; because he has little delusion, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of delusion. For him, these five supramundane faculties become eminent, sharp, and swift-moving. Which five? Namely: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. Because these five supramundane faculties are fulfilled, eminent, sharp, and swift-moving, he quickly touches the concentration that pierces the goal with speed—that is, for the destruction of the outflows.
This is called the pleasant practice, the path of purification. Monks, these are the four practices;
[they correspond to] the four cultivations of concentration.
In this regard, monks, what are the four cultivations of concentration?
(1) There is, monks, a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the abandonment of sensual desire.

(2) There is, monks, a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life. (3) There is, monks, a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision. (4) There is, monks, a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the attainment of wisdom. [23] In this regard, monks, what is the cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the abandoning of sensual desire?

In this case, monks, a monk—whether he is tranquil or has passed away, or whether he has gone to the charnel ground—contemplates this very body, from the soles of the feet upwards to the crown of the head, bounded by the skin and enclosed by the flesh, as it is situated and as it is disposed, full of various kinds of impurities. He reflects thoroughly:

"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, tears, sweat, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, urine, and the various types of grain."
Sweat and the like, urine, feces, excrement, pus, oiliness;

phlegm; saliva; nasal mucus; tears; vomit; marrow, fat, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, the head, and the brain—these are the various kinds of food and drink that fill the middle of the body, which is curved in its center. For example, it is like a double-walled vessel with openings at both ends through which [the contents] flow out.
A storehouse is filled with various kinds of grain belonging to six types of beings;
its four sides are made of wood, and there are subtle knowledges such as the *jāti* and others, as well as these coins and grains.
In the same way, monks, a monk examines this very body just as it is spread out, just as it has been directed, and so forth.
“Monks, this cultivation of concentration, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the abandonment of sensual desire.
(2) Now, monks, what is that cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to dwelling in happiness in the present life?

Here, monks, a monk—having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut—moistens, drenches, saturates, and suffuses this very body internally with the joy and happiness born of seclusion and born of concentration.”

In every respect, there is no part of his body that is not as if touched by the joy and bliss born of internal seclusion and born of concentration. Just as, monks, blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water-lilies, or white lotuses, born in the water, grown in the water, and level with the water, are all drenched, steeped, filled, saturated, and suffused with cool water; even so, monks, a monk who has gone to the foot of a tree or to an empty dwelling—
Or else, by means of this very absorption characterized by seclusion and accompanied by the joy and happiness of concentration, they calm, fill, purify, and pervade [the body].
For them, there is no obstruction anywhere in the body that prevents the radiance of the joy and happiness born of seclusion from suffusing it.
This cultivation of concentration, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
(2) In that regard, monks, what is the cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision?

In this regard, monks, a monk has properly, thoroughly, well-attended to, well-penetrated, and well-mastered the perception of light; he cultivates a mind of equal measure, overcoming the perception of night by means of the perception of day: as it is by day, so it is by night; as it is by night, so it is by day; as it was before, so it is after; as it is after, so it was before; as it was yesterday, so it is today; as it is today, so it will be in the future.
Thus, with a mind that is both wise and yet still mundane, one cultivates a consciousness of equal radiance designated by the term "day," which is uncreated by all agents.

Even there, in that state free from fear, during the three months of the terrifying [season] minus the three fortnights, at the time of midday when external signs have vanished and it is as pure as light—just as the previously described luminosity occurs and yet no conceptualization of "A" arises for him; even so, in that fearless state, the perception of light, which is devoid of qualities, becomes well-grasped, well-attended to, well-seen, and well-penetrated. He cultivates a mind of equal radiance designated by the perception of day: as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day; as before, so after; as after, so before; as today, so yesterday; and as yesterday, so tomorrow.
Thus, with a mind that is wise yet still mundane and designated by the notion of "day," one cultivates a mind of equal radiance.
This cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhibhāvanā*), when practiced, developed, and cultivated extensively, leads to the establishment of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*).

[28] (4) In this regard, the disciple asks: what is the cultivation of meditative concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated extensively at the outset, leads to the establishment of wisdom (*prajñā*)?

Here, a trainee who has entered training, or one who has mastered the training, or one who has gone beyond training—whether having abandoned the gross [hindrances] or having abandoned suffering—dwells, having attained and entered the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness, precisely because joy and dejection have already vanished.
This generation of concentration, when cultivated from the beginning, developed, and practiced extensively, conduces to the establishment of wisdom; thus, these are the generations of concentration.
(13) The four foundations of mindfulness.

In this regard, the disciple asks: "What are the four foundations of mindfulness? (1) Here, a monk—or indeed a nun—dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the body in the body externally. He dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world."

(2) He dwells contemplating feelings in internal feelings, in external feelings, and in both internal and external feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

(3) He dwells contemplating the mind in the internal mind, in the external mind, and in both internal and external mind—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

(4) He dwells contemplating phenomena in internal phenomena, in external phenomena, and in both internal and external phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
These, disciple, are the four foundations of mindfulness.
[25] The four right efforts:
(14) The Four Right Efforts.
In this regard, monks, what are the four right efforts?
(1) Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, takes hold of his mind, and applies himself correctly so that evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen do not arise.
(2) He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, upholds the mind, and applies right effort for the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states.
(3) He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, upholds the mind, and applies right effort for the arising of unarisen wholesome states.

(4) And for the stability, non-confusion, cultivation, increase, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen, he generates a complete desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, uplifts the mind, and applies himself correctly.
These, monks, are the four right efforts.
[30] (15) The four bases of psychic power.
In this regard, monks, what are the four bases of psychic power?

(1) Here, monks, a monk cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the concentration of desire and the formative forces of exertion, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; he will possess self-confidence and not lack confidence, nor will he be overly deluded.

(2) He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces predominant in energy and concentration, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; he will have confidence in himself, yet not excessive confidence, and will not be overly deluded.

(3) He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces predominant in mind and concentration, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; he will have confidence in himself, yet not excessive confidence, and will not be overly deluded. [31]

(4) By means of the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness—which are fully equipped with the six bases of investigation—he becomes certain of discernment, certain of dispassion, certain of the desire to cross over, and certain of perseverance; thus his investigation will neither be overly withdrawn nor overly dull.
These are the four faculties of training.
(16) The five faculties.
In that regard, the training: what are the five faculties?
Namely—(1) the faculty of faith, (2) the faculty of energy, (3) the faculty of mindfulness, (4) the faculty of concentration, and (5) the faculty of wisdom.
(1) Among these, what is the faculty of faith?

The faith by which one has faith in four things. Which four? One has faith in the mundane right view pertaining to the sphere of saṃsāra. One takes refuge in the ripening of karma, thinking: "Whatever karma I shall perform, whether wholesome or unwholesome, I shall experience the ripening of that very karma.
Even for the sake of one's life, one does not perform an unwholesome deed.
This is called the faculty of faith.
(2) In that regard, what is the faculty of energy?
Those phenomena which one will have faith in by means of the faculty of faith, those very phenomena one brings to fulfillment by means of the faculty of energy.
This is called the faculty of energy.
(3) In that regard, what is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?

Those phenomena which one brings to fulfillment by means of the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), those very phenomena one thoroughly attends to by means of the faculty of mindfulness. This is called the faculty of mindfulness.
(4) In that regard, what is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)?
Those phenomena which one does not thoroughly attend to by means of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), those phenomena one brings to one-pointedness by means of the faculty of concentration.
This is called the faculty of concentration.
(5) In that regard, what is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)?
Those phenomena which one makes one-pointed by means of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), those very phenomena one penetrates through the faculty of wisdom.
He becomes one whose nature is to examine them with equanimity.
This is called the faculty of wisdom. These are the five faculties of the trainee. (17) The five powers.
In that regard, what are the five powers of the trainee?
Namely: (1) the power of faith, (2) the power of energy, (3) the power of mindfulness, (4) the power of concentration, and (5) the power of wisdom.
These are the five powers of the trainee.
(18) The seven factors of enlightenment.
What are the seven factors of enlightenment for one training therein?

They are as follows: (1) the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, (2) the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, (3) the factor of enlightenment of energy, (4) the factor of enlightenment of joy, (5) the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, (6) the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and (7) the factor of enlightenment of equanimity. [34]
(1) Here, a disciple in training cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.

(2) In the same way, he cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
(3) He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is energy, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
(4) He cultivates the factor of awakening that is joy, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
(5) He cultivates the factor of awakening that is tranquility, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
(6) He cultivates the factor of awakening that is concentration, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
(7) He cultivates the factor of awakening that is equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
These, monks, are the seven factors of awakening. (19) The path is the yoke and the axle.
In this regard, monks, what is the path that leads to exertion?
It is the noble eightfold path, namely:
(1) right view, (2) right intention, (3) right speech, [and so forth].
(4) Right Action, (5) Right Livelihood, (6) Right Effort,
(7) Right Mindfulness, and (8) Right Concentration.
(1) In this regard, O learners, what is right view?
"There is this world; there is a world beyond; there is a mother; there is a father;

there is what is given; there is what is offered; there is the ripening of the fruit of deeds that are performed, whether desirable or undesirable, wholesome or unwholesome; and there are in this world those who have attained right knowledge and those who have practiced rightly."
O disciples, this is right view; its opposite is wrong view.
(2) What is right resolve?
It is ethical discipline and generosity dedicated toward the deeds of a Buddha and so forth, and not dedicated toward the eye, flesh, and so forth.
This, monks, is right intention.
(3) What is right speech? Here, monks, right speech is abstaining from harsh speech, false speech, slanderous speech, and frivolous chatter.
This is called right speech among the trainings.
(4) There are seven steps: what are they?
They are the engagement of body, speech, and mind in the ten courses of wholesome action.
In that regard, bodily [restraint] is threefold: abstaining from taking life, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.
Vocal [restraint] is fourfold: abstaining from false speech, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter.
Mental [restraint] is threefold: abstaining from covetousness, malice, and wrong view.

(ka) Therein, what is the taking of life? It is when there is a living being, one perceives it as a living being, one generates the intent to kill, one carries out the assault, and one deprives it of life.
This is called the definitive [definition] of taking life: it refers to objects of pride and conceit, except in cases of negligence. (b) What is taking what is not given?
Taking possession of another's property with a thieving mind is taking what is not given; except in the case of one's mother, father, or kinsmen.
Taking what belongs to friends, relatives, and others from their own hands when they are not away on a journey does not constitute taking what is not given.

(ga) Among these, what is sexual misconduct? It is approaching the wives of others or other men; all women who are forbidden by the king, those who are protected, those who are off-limits, and approaching them at an improper place or time [are included]. [37]
Now, the practice culminating in desire is explained. It is threefold in the month of Kārttika.
(a) What is falsehood?
Falsehood is speaking contrary to reality when asked about what has truly occurred; or, when not an Arhat, claiming "I am an Arhat," except in jest. Thus is falsehood defined.
(kha) What is malicious speech (*paiśunya*)? Malicious speech is that word which causes division, whether by means of what is untrue or what is true; thus is malicious speech defined.

(ga) What is harsh speech (*pāruṣya*)? Harsh speech is the causing of another to hear unpleasant words through the intent to inflict suffering upon them. That which causes another to hear unpleasant words with a mind characterized by natural compassion is not harsh speech. [38]
This is called the technical definition. (gha) What are the miscellaneous discourses?
They are as follows: discourse on kings, discourse on thieves, discourse on war, discourse on liquor, discourse on meat, discourse on women—
Whether one speaks of this or that talk concerning worldly gain, this is called mixed idle chatter (*sammisra-pralāpa*). One should not practice various kinds of unrighteousness.
(Ka) What is reliance on the diamond-like [samādhi] (*vajrāniśrayā*)?
Covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is the longing to make another's property one's own; it is defined as the thought, "May these goods belonging to another become mine.
(b) In that regard, what is ill-will (*vyāpāda*)?
The destruction, cutting off, and distraction caused by the venomous snake of malice, which is intent upon the ruin of the lives of others— this is called ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
(c) In that regard, what is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)?

"There is no this world; there is no other world," and so on as before. "This [false] view is threefold" (5). Among these, what is the view of self-aggrandizement? It consists of: success through festive celebrations and the like, deceitful behavior, seeking gain through signs, and the expectation of gain through asceticism, as well as the longing for gain through ostentation.

(a) In that regard, what is deceit (*kuhanā*)? Having seen a perfected one (*siddha*) or a festival and so forth, while sitting cross-legged on a new rug, he makes it known: "I am a meditator; may I meet with a perfected one. He thinks, "Thus there will be gain and honor for me. Such as this is called deceit.
(b) In that regard, what is hinting (*chaṇanā*)?

In this case, for the very purpose of gain, honor, and respect, one speaks such affectionate words as, "You are my mother," "You are my father," "You are my sister," "You are my daughter," and other similar pleasant expressions; this is called *chaṇanā* (flattery). (Ga) Among these, what is *naimittika* (hinting)? It is when, having purified one's alms-food at a festival for those who have attained spiritual success (*siddhi*) and so forth, one says with a non-meager intention: "Such is this alms-food as it is found among those of great prosperity; it is not obtained among those who lack such wealth. However, there is no possibility [of such flattery] for one who speaks out of a desire for little honor.
Thus is called the occasional begging bowl (*naimittika-sam*).

(Gha) In that regard, what is the lifelong begging bowl (*naiṣṭhikika-sam*)? A monk, at whatever house he does not receive alms-food, such that it becomes like ashes scattered by inheritance, there he says: [40]
"Those who take the side of non-giving go to hell; you too, being on the side of non-giving, will go to hell.
Thus addressed, they, filled with fear and dread, offered almsfood.
Having obtained that, they consume it.
This is called the naiṣādikavṛtta (the way of the hunter).
(ḍa) In that regard, what is the seeking of gain through gain?
A monk, using his own abundant wealth, showed beautiful robes to the Caulakiya lay followers, saying, "We obtain robes such as these.
They were ashamed and gave whatever robes they had; he made use of those.
Thus, monks, is described the desire for gain through gain on the part of a monk;
this is the wrong livelihood of a monk.
Right livelihood is that which is far removed from such [desire].
(And) here indeed, monks, for a lay follower, wrong livelihood consists in:

the sale of poison, the sale of weapons, the sale of living beings, the sale of intoxicants, the sale of meat, and the sale of choice sesame and mustard seeds procured by improper means— this is wrong livelihood.
Fifty and a half.
[41] Now, the *sampragalbī* [breaths] are described.
Among them, what is the *sampragalbī*?
In this context, the ritual of the *bhiṣu* sacrifice must be performed as a subsidiary act (*aṅga*) of the *abhicāra-naivedya-anuṣṭhāna*, involving the proper conduct of the fingers.
Now, the *bhiṣu* sacrifice of the *sampragalvī* [type] is described.
(7) In that regard, what is the *sampragalvī* performance of the *bhiṣu* sacrifice?

In this world, indeed, when a physician sees another physician or a woman, whether during a festival or in the case of illness, he examines both the external and internal parts of the body as one who perceives things as they truly are: namely, the hair of the head, the body hair, the nails, the teeth, dirt, filth, skin, flesh, bone, sinew, veins, and kidneys.
The heart, the spleen, the liver, the gallbladder, the stomach, the large intestine, the small intestines, the mesentery, the kidneys, feces, the temporal bone, sweat, saliva,
nasal mucus, muscle fat, lymph, marrow, adipose tissue, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, the brain, the membrane of the skull, and excrement and urine.
"It is full of various kinds of impurity"—
thus right mindfulness is cultivated.
(8) What is right concentration?

There are four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first *dhyāna*, which is accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in a state without applied or sustained thought.

Having attained and dwelling in the second dhyāna, which is the joy and happiness born of concentration; and through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly conscious, experiencing happiness with the body— of which the Noble Ones say, "He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous"— he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna.

Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the previous disappearance of mental joy and mental grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. These, monks, are indeed the four dhyānas.
This is called right concentration.
This, monks, is the noble eightfold path.
[Next is] mindfulness of breathing in sixteen aspects.

In this regard, monks, what is mindfulness of breathing in its sixteen aspects? Here, monks, a monk, when inhaling, understands as it truly is: "I am inhaling"; when exhaling, he understands as it truly is: "I am exhaling.
When inhaling deeply, he understands as it truly is: "I am inhaling deeply"; when exhaling deeply, he understands as it truly is: "I am exhaling deeply."

(1) When inhaling long, he understands as it really is: "I am inhaling long"; or when exhaling long, he understands as it really is: "I am exhaling long. (2) When inhaling short, he understands as it really is: "I am inhaling short"; or when exhaling short, he understands as it really is: "I am exhaling short."

(3) Experiencing all bodily formations, while there is an outflow, he understands as it really is: "Experiencing all bodily formations, I am experiencing an outflow. Experiencing all bodily formations, while there is no outflow, he understands as it really is: "Experiencing all bodily formations, I am experiencing no outflow. (4) Experiencing rapture, while there is an outflow, he understands: "Experiencing rapture, I am experiencing an outflow. [14a]

He understands it as it truly is: when experiencing joy while breathing in, he understands as it truly is, "I am experiencing joy while breathing in"; when breathing out, he understands as it truly is, "I am experiencing joy while breathing out. Or, when experiencing pleasure while breathing in, he understands according to the Sūtra, "I am experiencing pleasure while breathing in"; when breathing out, he understands according to the Sūtra, "I am experiencing pleasure while breathing out."

(6) Calming the bodily formations while breathing in, he understands as it is in the Sūtra: "Calming the bodily formations, I am breathing in. Calming the bodily formations while breathing out, he understands as it is in the Sūtra: "Calming the bodily formations, I am breathing out. (7) Experiencing the mental formations while breathing in, he understands as it is in the Sūtra: "Experiencing the mental formations, I am breathing in."
Experiencing mental formations while breathing out, he understands as it is in the Sūtra: "Experiencing mental formations, I am breathing out.

(8) Calming mental formations while breathing in, he understands as it is in the Sūtra: "Calming mental formations, I am breathing in. Calming mental formations while breathing out, he understands as it is in the Sūtra: "Calming mental formations, I am breathing out."

(9) Experiencing the mind while inhaling, he understands as it is in the sūtra: "Experiencing the mind, I am inhaling. Experiencing the mind while exhaling, he understands as it is in the sūtra: "Experiencing the mind, I am exhaling.
(10) Gladdening my mind while inhaling, he understands as it is in the sūtra: "Gladdening my mind, I am inhaling."
Gladdening the mind while breathing out, he understands as it is in the Sūtra: "Gladdening the mind, I am breathing out.

(11) Composing the mind while breathing in, he understands as it is in the Sūtra: "Composing the mind, I am breathing in. Composing the mind while breathing out, he understands as it is in the Sūtra: "Composing the mind, I am breathing out."
(12) While breathing in while liberating the mind, he understands as it is in the Sūtra: "I am breathing in while liberating the mind.
While breathing out while liberating the mind, he understands as it is in the Sūtra: "I am breathing out while liberating the mind.
[44] These are the four currents and the eight factors.

(13) He understands as it really is: "They say there is the contemplation of the five [aggregates], (14) the contemplation of dispassion, (15) the contemplation of cessation, and (16) the contemplation of relinquishment; they say that the contemplation of relinquishment is infinite; 'I am one who possesses the contemplation of relinquishment'—he understands this as it really is. Or, regarding the non-manifestation of relinquishment, he understands as it really is: 'They say there is the contemplation of relinquishment that is hidden; I am one who possesses the contemplation of relinquishment that is hidden.'"
This, monks, is the mindfulness of breathing for Poṭṭhapāda.
(21) There are four streams and eight factors.
In this regard, monks, what are the four streams and eight factors?

(1) Here, monks, a noble disciple has full confidence in the Buddha through his fearlessness, thinking: "That Blessed One is indeed the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. (2) Through his fearlessness regarding the Dharma, he has full confidence, thinking: "The Dharma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise."

Namely: the crushing of intoxication, the subduing of thirst, the cessation of delusion, the cutting off of pride, the calming of hypocrisy, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and nirvāṇa.

(2) Together with the removal of negligence, he becomes possessed of clear comprehension. A disciple of the Blessed One is one who has well crossed over, who has entered upon the right way, who has entered upon the straight way, who has entered upon the proper way, and who has entered upon the way that accords with the Dharma. [47]

There are those who have practiced what they heard; there are those who, in this very life, are candidates for the realization of the fruit of the state of a Stream-enterer (*srotāpatti-phala-sākṣātkriyā*), and there are those who are Stream-enterers; there are those who, in this very life, are candidates for the realization of the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala-sākṣātkriyā*), and there are those who are Once-returners; there are those who, in this very life, are candidates for the realization of the fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmi-phala-sākṣātkriyā*), and there are those who are Non-returners; there are those who, in this very life, are candidates for the realization of the fruit of Arhatship (*arhat-phala-sākṣātkriyā*).
There are six types of Arhats; namely—the four "flower-like" individuals (*puṣpa-pudgala*) and the two "flower-like" persons (*puṣpa-pudgala*).

Such is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples: endowed with hearing, endowed with concentration, endowed with faith, endowed with learning, endowed with liberation, and endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation; worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, and worthy of reverential salutation with joined palms.

He is one who should be followed; he is the unsurpassed field of merit, worthy of offerings from the world. (4) Regarding solitude: he is clearly conscious of those dwellings which are unbroken, flawless, unblemished, irreproachable, incomparable, and peerless.
He explains those that are not yet fully grown, those that are tender, those that are well-guarded, those praised by the wise, and those that have been properly cultivated.
These are the three types of trees and the five supramundane aggregates. [48]
(22) The ten powers of a Tathāgata.
In this regard, monks, what are the ten powers of a Tathāgata?
(1) Here, monks, a Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.
(2) He understands, as it truly is, the ripening of the undertaking of karmic actions belonging to the past, future, and present.
(3) He understands, as it truly is, the path leading everywhere, along with its cessation, for those with various inclinations and various dispositions.
(4) He understands, as it truly is, the world of manifold elements and the world of diverse elements.
(5) He understands, as it truly is, the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings. (6) He understands, as it truly is, the path that leads everywhere.
(7) [The knowledge] of the faculties of all sentient beings—[69]
For those who have attained the lower meditative attainments (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*), he teaches the concise and detailed explanation of their bases according to the Sūtra.

(8) Furthermore, he recollects his various former lives with their modes, details, and characteristics; he recollects his previous existence, whether as one birth, two births, or even many hundreds of thousands of millions of births—this is the full account.

(9) Furthermore, with his purified divine eye, which transcends that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn; he knows, in detail, how they are reborn in happy or miserable destinies according to their good or evil conduct of body, speech, and mind.
(10) Through wisdom, he directs the turning of the mind toward conversion and attraction, as prescribed in the sūtras.
These, monks, are the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
(23) The four grounds of self-confidence.
In this regard, monks, what are the four grounds of self-confidence of the Tathāgata?
(1) Here, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, declares of himself: [I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one].

"If anyone in this world— including its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, princes and men— should say, 'These phenomena have not been fully awakened to,' I would recognize that as being like a mere sign. Because I do not perceive such a sign, I dwell in security and remain vigilant."
He understands the proper place as a mirror.

From a correct exposition, he roars the lion’s roar and urges on the brahmin, whether unurged or not led by the brahmin, or indeed by anyone else who has dwelt according to the Dharma. Furthermore, regarding those qualities of inner taming that have been proclaimed for him, while he practices them, there is no fear of being dragged away by others in that matter; this is the detailed explanation.

(3) Furthermore, those practices which one undertakes that are noble and leading to liberation—if, while practicing them, they do not lead to liberation for one who acts accordingly, nor to the complete destruction of suffering, nor to the goal [of the path], then the meaning is as previously explained regarding the state of being dragged away. [51] “From that, he perceives his own [defilements]; declaring ‘these of mine are not yet exhausted,’ he speaks with this meaning. All these, having ascended together in the world, having followed together, among the seven classes of beings, always favoring [them], he perceives this as the cause of wealth.”
Observing the signs as they follow him, he dwells having attained security as he came, yet not having attained [final] patience.

He understands the first position; having entered upon the path, he roars the lion’s roar: "I turn the wheel that has not been turned by any ascetic or brahmin, nor by anyone else in the world, in accordance with the Dharma.
These are the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*).
(24) The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
In this regard, what are the Tathāgata’s four analytical knowledges?

They are as follows: (1) the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), (2) the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), (3) the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and (4) the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).

(1) What is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*)? It is as follows: "The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is that non-retrogressive knowledge. (2) What is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*)?

The dharma that is not to be known is the irreversible knowledge. (3) What is the analytical knowledge of etymological interpretation (*niruktipratisaṃvid*)? It is the irreversible knowledge regarding verbal expression.

(4) What is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)? It is the irreversible knowledge regarding the possession of logical and fluent speech, the mastery of meditative concentration, and the answering of questions.
These are the analytical knowledges according to their literal definition.

(25) Now, as for the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikā buddhadharmāḥ*): what are those eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? They are as follows: (1) the Tathāgata has no physical lapse; (2) he has no vocal outcry; (3) he has no loss of mindfulness; (4) he has no unconcentrated mind; (5) he has no perception of diversity; (6) he has no equanimity lacking discernment; (7) there is no decline in his zeal (*chanda*); (8) there is no decline in his vigor (*vīrya*).

(9) there is no loss of mindfulness, (10) there is no loss of concentration, (11) there is no loss of wisdom, (12) there is no loss of liberation; (13) unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past, (14) unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the future, (15) unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the present; (16) all bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.
(17) All verbal action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge. (18) All mental action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.
These are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikā buddhadharmāḥ*).
(29) The thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇāni*).

In that regard, what are the thirty-two marks of a great person (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇāni*) of the Tathāgata? Accordingly, he will state immediately thereafter: "In that regard, monks, what are the five aggregates of clinging? and so on.
From this it is known that the aggregates of form and so forth, which are the objects of clinging (upādāna), are taught here.
For these noble ones, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of that form which is not for the sake of a self, rooted in ignorance, and belonging to the perfected yogin.

Whatever sensation (*vedanā*) is in that collection, that is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*). Whatever perception (*saṃjñā*) is in that [collection], that is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).

Excluding feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā), the remaining mental factors— faith and the others— are associated with that [consciousness], while the formations such as birth and so forth are dissociated from it.
Furthermore, consciousness is here described as belonging to the category of consciousness-formations (vijñāna-skandha).
"And from the formations conditioned by consciousness"— if this were not so, the phrase would not be consistent;
thus the word "iti" (thus) concludes the section.
"Of these, [it is said]: 'These five physicians are for the sake of the [five] constituents'.

(2) Regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*), there is the question beginning with "In that regard, Siddhatra," for the purpose of explaining the aggregates of clinging. Therein, the word *tatra* is used to introduce the sentence; *siddhatra* is a form of address. The mention of the number "five" is intended to demonstrate that there are exactly five aggregates, thereby precluding both deficiency and excess, and to exclude other categories such as the six elements (*dhātu*) or the twelve bases (*āyatana*). Generally, they say that among the [eighteen] elements (*tattva*), the aggregate of consciousness alone is not included [among the aggregates of clinging]. Among the objects of attachment, such as form and so forth, there is no further grasping beyond those. Therefore, there are only five aggregates.

Regarding the term "appropriation-aggregates" (*upādānaskandha*): I shall explain what is appropriated (*upādāna*). The aggregates that are designated by that [term] are "appropriation-aggregates. This is due to the elision of the middle term, as in the words *druṇa*, *vṛṣaga*, and *himavat*. Others establish this through a bahuvrīhi compound with elision of the middle term, such as *maṅgākṣa*. Alternatively, the aggregates of the appropriations are "appropriation-aggregates. And thus the etymological derivation (*nirukta*) is established: it is like saying "the thirst for impermanent things" (*anityatṛṣṇā*). It is indeed stated in the treatise on the enumeration of sentient beings (*sattvasaṃkhyāśāstra*) that these are the appropriation-aggregates; I shall explain this further. Now, because they are the cause of the sequence of the members [of dependent origination], how are entities [called] appropriation-aggregates according to the statement?
They too are delighted by grasping (*upādāna*), because it is described that "the variety of the world is born of karma.
Alternatively, it is due to the distinction of specific types of grasping, like a "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*).
Just as a person who is distinguished by a king is a "king's man."

Thus is the distinction among the appropriations: that of form, and those of the aggregates of appropriation. Their characteristic is understood from their cause, or from their activity; and there is also contact among them.
Regarding the aggregates of form and appropriation, there are the sense-faculties and the aggregate of appropriation.
Among these, the aggregate of form consists of the five sense-faculties,
such as the eye, and the twenty-five objects, such as visible form.
The aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) consists of pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Furthermore, it is sixfold, comprising the six groups of feeling born of visual contact, up to those born of mental contact.
As for the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), it is the discernment of signs such as blue, yellow, long, short, and so forth.
And like feeling (*vedanā*), there are "the six groups of perception" (*saṃjñākāya*).

Furthermore, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) consists of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [states], as well as those that are associated and dissociated, and those that are acquired and unacquired; in brief, the formations are summarized by these very concise terms.
Its essential nature is consciousness colored by objects such as form and so forth.
Furthermore, that consciousness consists of the six groups of consciousness, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
What is the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*)? It has the sense of a "heap. Why is this so? Because of the Sūtra.

This is because of the statement: "Whatever accumulation exists in an accumulated state— whether internal or external, coarse or subtle, inferior or superior, whether far or near— all that, when condensed into a single portion, receives the designation 'form-aggregate' (rūpaskandha)."
Therefore, it is established that the meaning of "heap" (*skandha*) is the meaning of "collection" (*rāśi*). In this way, the three [other] aggregates should also be understood.
Now, why is it said that "only form is experienced"?

(1) According to their relative grossness (*yathaudārikatena*). How so? Form (*rūpa*) is indeed the grossest of all because it is most easily perceived. Feeling (*vedanā*) is grosser than the [other] aggregates because its activity is gross; for instance, when one is afflicted, one says, "There is a feeling in my hand," or "There is a feeling in my foot. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is grosser than the formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*); and formations are grosser than consciousness. Therefore, they are listed in that order according to their relative grossness.

(2) Or [the order is] according to the process of defilement (*saṃkleśataḥ*). For in beginningless *saṃsāra*, within the afflicted states, form (*rūpa*) is the basis for one another. And those [afflictions] follow from the nature of volition (*caitanya*). Its production is due to the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*). The perversion of perception arises from entities (*vastu*). And the remainder is defiled by them; thus, the sequence is according to the process of defilement. (3) Or [the order is] according to the sense of being a "vessel" (*bhājana*). Form is like a vessel because it serves as the support for volition and the rest. Feeling (*vedanā*) is like food because of its quality of being tasted. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is self-existent, because by grasping signs (*nimitta*), it establishes the state of volition and the others. Thus [it is said].
Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are so called because they form the consciousness (*vijñāna*) for rebirth by preparing it through their own ripening;
consciousness is designated as the "experiencer" because of its association with that [volitional formation].
[116] (3) The eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Having taught the elements within the context of the five aggregates of clinging, he said: "In that regard, what are the eighteen elements?

Here, the Blessed One has taught the elements by way of the distinct characteristics of the basis (*āśraya*) and that which is based upon it (*āśrita*). Among these, the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and the consciousness-element (*vijñānadhātu*) constitute the basis; the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) constitute that which is based upon it.

The bases consist of the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). The sixfold group beginning with the eye should be understood as the internal [bases]. It is said that by that very sequence, the sequence of their respective objects and consciousness-elements is established: (1) the prior mention of the five elements beginning with the mind-element (*manodhātu*) which is constant.
Because its object is present; the object of the mind (*manas*) is unrestricted: some [mental objects] have the present as their object, while others have the past and future as their objects.
Furthermore, the elements of the body (*kāyadhātu*) and the four [faculties] beginning with the eye are mentioned first because their objects are derived matter (*bhautika*).
However, the object of the body is unrestricted: in some cases it consists of primary elements (*bhūta*), and in other cases it consists of derived matter.

In some cases, there is no fear. Among the nose, tongue, eye, and ear, the first three [the nose, tongue, and eye] do not reach their objects because they perceive objects that have already passed away.

The operation of the nose and the tongue is not considered "distant" because they grasp objects that have already reached them. Furthermore, the operation of the eye functions at a greater distance than even the ear; for instance, one hears the sound of a thundering cloud even when it is five *yojanas* away. The ear was mentioned previously as being more distant than the tongue. The nose was mentioned again after the tongue because it lacks the quality of smelling; for if the tongue were to smell, it would cause liberation.

(2) Alternatively, in this body, the location of the eye is situated at the top; below that is the location of the ear; below that is the location of the nose; below that is the location of the tongue; and below that is the location of the body for the most part. As for the mind, it is designated as being determined by those very [faculties]. Now, the definition of the eye and the others is stated: the eye is the basis of visual consciousness, having the purpose of perceiving visible forms.
It is translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*). By this, the ear and the other [senses] are also explained. This much is the distinction here:

[the question] "Why are they called 'translucent matter' because their function is seeing and so forth, rather than being the support? [The answer is: "By way of their lineage (*gotra*) and so forth. But what is the "mind-eye" (*citta-cakṣus*)? [It is] by way of the lineages and so forth.

Just as when a single mountain possesses many types of mineral ores such as silver and trees, they are called "elements" (*dhātu*), so too, within a single continuum (*santāna*) or basis (*āśraya*), the eighteen lineages (*gotra*) are called the "eighteen elements.

Furthermore, these lineages are not called [elements] because of their essential nature (*ākāra-tattva*). Rather, what are the eyes and so forth that are described as the forms (*ākāra*) of those [lineages]? They are the forms of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
For it is because these minds and mental factors arise from causes and conditions that they are also called "elements" (*dhātu*).
The elements have been explained. [116] (4) The twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Immediately following that, he states what is to be explained: the question, "Which are the twelve bases (*āyatana*)?

and the response, "The eye is an internal base. Now, since there is no self (*ātman*), how can the eye be considered internal on account of its existence [within it]? For even though they are located in the head, cold veins are not established as being the head itself.

It is like a basis (*āśraya*). However, because they are superimposed upon the support of the ego-grasping (*ahaṅkāra*), they are called "bases" starting from the eye. And since that [basis] is the support for the ego-grasping of the mind, it is designated by the term "superimposition. That alone is the internal [basis]. It is internal precisely because it is superimposed. When the mind is metaphorically designated as being close [to the sense organ], it arises depending on the eye as its basis.
The cause for internal inclination is explained; it is what is meant by the "basis of consciousness. The eyes and so forth are fully enumerated.
The objects are now described: form is twofold, consisting of color and shape. [96]
Sound is of two kinds:
that which has a material cause as its basis, such as the characteristic of a drum; and that which does not have a material cause as its basis, such as the sound of wind, falling trees, or a river.
This is the definition of sound.
Sound possesses two qualities: good quality and bad quality, according to whether it is produced by a similar or dissimilar effort.
Taste is of six kinds, distinguished as sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.

This tangible object (*spraṣṭavya*) is of eleven kinds: the fourfold element-fire (*dhātupāvaka*), roughness and so forth, lightness, cold, natural flavor (*nijarasa*), and thirst. As for "and so forth" (*ādi*), it refers to hardness, softness, heaviness, and fluidity. "Cold" (*śīta*) is that which produces a sensation of coolness when touched. "Natural flavor" (*nijarasa*) is the taste inherent in things such as roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits, and tubers. "Thirst" (*pipāsā*) is the desire for water. These are the eleven types of tangible objects. Furthermore, these eleven types of tangible objects are subsumed within the three great elements (*mahābhūta*). Among them, the fourfold element-fire is the fire-element (*tejo-dhātu*). Roughness and so forth are the earth-element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). Lightness is the wind-element (*vāyu-dhātu*). Cold is the water-element (*ap-dhātu*). Natural flavor and thirst are included within the water-element. Thus, all eleven types of tangible objects are comprised within the three great elements. Regarding the fourfold element-fire: "element" (*dhātu*) means the constituent part (*avayava*) of the body. "Fire" (*pāvaka*) means that which burns (*pacati*). It is called "fourfold" because it consists of the four types: digestive fire (*pariṇāmāgni*), metabolic heat (*santāpanāgni*), the fire of the sense-faculties (*indriyāgni*), and the fire of the life-force (*jīvāgni*). Among these, digestive fire is that which digests the food and drink consumed by beings. Metabolic heat is that which maintains the body's warmth. The fire of the sense-faculties is that which sustains the clarity of the sense-faculties. The fire of the life-force is that which maintains the life-span. This is the meaning of the fourfold element-fire. Furthermore, the fourfold element-fire is further divided into eight types: the fire of digestion, the fire of maturation, the fire of transformation, the fire of burning, the fire of cooking, the fire of the sense-faculties, the fire of the life-force, and the fire of the great elements. Among these, the fire of digestion is that which digests the food and drink consumed by beings. The fire of maturation is that which matures the fetus in the womb. The fire of transformation is that which transforms the various bodily constituents. The fire of burning is that which burns external objects. The fire of cooking is that which cooks external objects. The fire of the sense-faculties is that which sustains the clarity of the sense-faculties. The fire of the life-force is that which maintains the life-span. The fire of the great elements is that which maintains the great elements. This is the meaning of the eightfold division of the fourfold element-fire. Furthermore, the fourfold element-fire is further divided into twelve types: the fire of digestion, the fire of maturation, the fire of transformation, the fire of burning, the fire of cooking, the fire of the sense-faculties, the fire of the life-force, the fire of the great elements, the fire of the internal organs, the fire of the limbs, the fire of the joints, and the fire of the vital points. Among these, the fire of digestion is as previously described. The fire of maturation is as previously described. The fire of transformation is that which transforms the various bodily constituents. The fire of burning is that which burns external objects. The fire of cooking is that which cooks external objects. The fire of the sense-faculties is as previously described. The fire of the life-force is as previously described. The fire of the great elements is as previously described. The fire of the internal organs is that which resides in the stomach and other internal organs. The fire of the limbs is that which resides in the hands, feet, and other limbs. The fire of the joints is that which resides in the joints of the hands, feet, and other limbs. The fire of the vital points is that which resides in the heart and other vital points. This is the meaning of the twelvefold division of the fourfold element-fire. Furthermore, the fourfold element-fire is further divided into sixteen types: the fire of digestion, the fire of maturation, the fire of transformation, the fire of burning, the fire of cooking, the fire of the sense-faculties, the fire of the life-force, the fire of the great elements, the fire of the internal organs, the fire of the limbs, the fire of the joints, the fire of the vital points, the fire of the channels, the fire of the pores, and the fire of the skin. Among these, the first twelve are as previously described. The fire of the channels is that which flows through the channels. The fire of the pores is that which resides in the pores. The fire of the skin is that which resides in the skin. This is the meaning of the sixteenfold division of the fourfold element-fire.
