Furthermore, the fourfold element-fire is further divided into twenty types: the fire of digestion, the fire of maturation, the fire of transformation, the fire of burning, the fire of cooking, the fire of the sense-faculties, the fire of the life-force, the fire of the great elements, the fire of the internal organs, the fire of the limbs, the fire of the joints, the fire of the vital points, the fire of the channels, the fire of the pores, the fire of the skin, the fire of the blood, the fire of the flesh, the fire of the fat, the fire of the bone, and the fire of the marrow. Among these, the first sixteen are as previously described. The fire of the blood is that which resides in the blood. The fire of the flesh is that which resides in the flesh. The fire of the fat is that which resides in the fat. The fire of the bone is that which resides in the bones. The fire of the marrow is that which resides in the marrow. This is the meaning of the twentyfold division of the fourfold element-fire. Furthermore, the fourfold element-fire is further divided into twenty-four types: the fire of digestion, the fire of maturation, the fire of transformation, the fire of burning, the fire of cooking, the fire of the sense-faculties, the fire of the life-force, the fire of the great elements, the fire of the internal organs, the fire of the limbs, the fire of the joints, the fire of the vital points, the fire of the channels, the fire of the pores, the fire of the skin, the fire of the blood, the fire of the flesh, the fire of the fat, the fire of the bone, the fire of the marrow, the fire of the sinews, the fire of the tendons, the fire of the nerves, and the fire of the veins. Among these, the first twenty are as previously described. The fire of the sinews is that which resides in the sinews. The fire of the tendons is that which resides in the tendons. The fire of the nerves is that which resides in the nerves. The fire of the veins is that which resides in the veins. This is the meaning of the twenty-fourfold division of the fourfold element-fire. Furthermore, the fourfold element-fire is further divided into thirty-two types: the fire of digestion, the fire of maturation, the fire of transformation, the fire of burning, the fire of cooking, the fire of the sense-faculties, the fire of the life-force, the fire of the great elements, the fire of the internal organs, the fire of the limbs, the fire of the joints, the fire of the vital points, the fire of the channels, the fire of the pores, the fire of the skin, the fire of the blood, the fire of the flesh, the fire of the fat, the fire of the bone, the fire of the marrow, the fire of the sinews, the fire of the tendons, the fire of the nerves, the fire of the veins, the fire of the arteries, the fire of the capillaries, the fire of the sweat, the fire of the tears, the fire of the saliva, and the fire of the phlegm. Among these, the first thirty are as previously described. The fire of the sweat is that which resides in the sweat. The fire of the tears is that which resides in the tears. The fire of the saliva is that which resides in the saliva. The fire of the phlegm is that which resides in the phlegm. This is the meaning of the thirty-twofold division of the fourfold element-fire. Furthermore, the fourfold element-fire is further divided into forty types: the fire of digestion, the fire of maturation, the fire of transformation, the fire of burning, the fire of cooking, the fire of the sense-faculties, the fire of the life-force, the fire of the great elements, the fire of the internal organs, the fire of the limbs, the fire of the joints, the fire of the vital points, the fire of the channels, the fire of the pores, the fire of the skin, the fire of the blood, the fire of the flesh, the fire of the fat, the fire of the bone, the fire of the marrow, the fire of the sinews, the fire of the tendons, the fire of the nerves, the fire of the veins,

The teaching of the Dharma is the aggregate that provides instruction on feeling (*vedanā*). Space, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and inconceivable transformation—these are the seven substances.

[97] What are the bases (*āyatana*)? They are the two: the cognizer (*cijña*) and the knowable (*jñeya*). For the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of "bases" is: they extend (*tanvanti*) the duality of the cognizer and the knowable.
"Tanvanti" means they extend or spread out. Here, the bases (āyatana) are explained.
Following this is the exposition of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). Regarding that, it is said: therein, which [is it]?

"Dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and so forth. Now, what is the meaning of "dependent origination"? It is said: it means the establishment of a connection. The meaning is "arising from this"; the meaning is "by way of being established. That is said to have the sense of "inherence" (*samavāya*); the prefix *prati* has the sense of "manifestation. This is what is meant: [the arising] of things in relation to their respective collections of causes.

"Dependent origination is arising by way of inherence. To show the sequence [of the members] starting from the activity established in relation to objects such as the aggregates, he says: "Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces (*saṃskārāḥ*). This means that ignorance is the condition, i.e., the cause, of those [formative forces].
These are conditioned by ignorance; that is to say, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) have ignorance as their cause. The same applies to other factors of this kind.

Furthermore, within this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), three members consist of the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*): ignorance, craving, and grasping; one member is intended as impure karma: the formative forces and existence (*bhava*); and seven members consist of the nature of entities (*vastu*): consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death, because they have afflictions and karma as their causes.

And therein, because ignorance is the cause of the fourfold [set of factors], saṃsāra manifests; and because old age and death are fruitless in their fourfold nature, there is an end [to the cycle]. Alternatively, another factor would have to be sought for that which has been discarded, and yet another for that one as well—thus there would be an infinite regress.
There is no state of being neither [the one nor the other], because the Blessed One has shown the protections.
From affliction, affliction is said to arise: from craving, grasping arises.
From affliction comes karma; from grasping comes becoming; from ignorance come volitional formations.

From karma comes the objective basis; from volitional formations comes consciousness, and from that, birth. From the objective basis also comes the objective basis; from consciousness comes what is situated in the self, and from birth come aging and death.
Affliction also arises from the object: namely, craving arises from sensation.
Since the detailed explanation of the three links of existence is thus complete, it is thereby made known that affliction also arises from the object due to the presence of affliction.
Furthermore, affliction arises again from the cause of aging and death, which consists of sensation and craving.
In this regard, there is nothing contradictory in stating: "Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering. For otherwise, what would be its functional efficacy?

In another Sūtra, it is said that ignorance is the fuel for improper mental attention: "Improper mental attention has ignorance as its cause. And that [ignorance] becomes associated with other distinctions within grasping; thus it is complete.

And here, five members are of the nature of causes; ignorance, formations, craving, grasping, and existence are, as appropriate, of the nature of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). The remaining members are co-nascent and are of the nature of results. [Objection: But has not dependent origination been explained here in the *Pūrvapakṣasaṃsāntvavyūha* as "What is dependent origination? All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)"? Yet in the Sūtra, it is stated that it pertains only to those called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). [Response: This is because this explanation of the seal (*mudrā*) is intended for sentient beings.

The state called "Reality" (tattva), which is the ground accessible only through non-investigation and is devoid of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), was taught by the Blessed One for the sake of certain disciples who wander in saṃsāra under the influence of Īśvara, in order to eliminate the delusion of their adherence to a permanent cause.
The meaning is that it is the summit of the view of defining characteristics, because it is free from all defining characteristics.

Sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair arise; therein, the transformation of the object known as the "existent entity" does not occur through the transformation of its non-dual state of being.
Sorrow (*śoka*) is the internal burning based on the perceived objects of the mind and so forth. Lamentation (*parideva*) is the shedding of tears due to that sorrow. [102]
This will be explained later.
"Fatigue" refers to fasting, which indicates grief and lamentation;
the same logic should be applied to other cases as well by means of analogy.

In the state of isolation (kaivalya), for one who is devoid of the thought "I am isolated," there is the great height of the mass of suffering; here, "mass of suffering" refers to a collection of sufferings. "Arising occurs" is the initial statement.
Having thus explained the process of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), he speaks of the activity of the mind (*cittavṛtti*).
The detailed explanation begins with "through connection with ignorance and so forth" and "due to the cessation of formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth.
Thus, one who has entered into this understanding of non-activity becomes one who knows dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Why, moreover, does one experience the sensation of dependent origination through these two types of differentiation?
It is said:
because of this differentiation among those to be trained.
For the dispositions of those to be trained (*vineya*) are diverse; thus, some are suitable for a particular method of guidance.

Among these, the one that conforms to the process of worldly existence—namely, "how this saṃsāra proceeds"—is established among those to be trained as the subject matter concerning the process of existence (*pravṛtti-krama*), for the purpose of demonstrating that very process.
The reverse order, however, is intended for those desiring penetration, for the purpose of demonstrating penetration.
Therefore, teaching in both ways, he brings the discussion to a conclusion with the words "as the teaching," [stating that] one would attain the conviction of those to be trained.
Is ignorance merely ignorance alone, or is it in every respect among these [categories] through the [four] types of non-explanation?
Therefore, regarding the progression of the question: "What is ignorance (*avidyā*) therein?
it is said that it is the non-relinquishing of those things that are not the path, and the lack of knowledge regarding what has been repeated.
By means of the classification of ignorance, he demonstrates its objective support (*ālambana*), its pervasive support (*paryālamba*), and its divisions.
"Repetition and so forth" refers to the self;

"ignorance and so forth" are its synonyms. "Repetition" is the past birth. In that regard, "ignorance" is [the thought] "What was I in the past time? and so forth; "doubt" is [the inquiry] regarding that same matter.

The future birth is the "subsequent limit. Ignorance regarding that consists of doubts such as: "Shall I exist in the future time? and so forth. The present birth is the "current" one. Ignorance regarding that consists of doubts such as: "What is this? and "Who am I? and so forth. On the earth, there is delusion consisting of doubt regarding the earth itself, which arises from a lack of discernment.
By this, ignorance itself is non-discrimination (*aviveka*),
being the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*), just like a non-friend (*amitra*) and so forth.

And it is shown by the phrase "and from the storehouse through experience" that there is ignorance regarding what lies beyond the city. This refers to the ignorance concerning suffering, which proceeds as if it were non-different [from the self].
Or, for one who imagines [the self] as prior, there is neither the previously mentioned [self] nor that which is established by the meaning;
"the person is only as far as the range of the senses" refers to ignorance regarding the internal.

Ignorance regarding one's own continuum with respect to the fourfold [truths] is as follows: ignorance regarding the self, regarding objects, regarding what is desired, and regarding liberation; likewise, ignorance regarding external objects is [ignorance] concerning sorrow.
The meaning of "external" (bāhya) is that which is to be known through another particle; it is the lack of knowledge regarding anything other than one's own continuum.
The unique [ignorance] is that which is devoid of distress and grief;
this too is ignorance, because it functions as the basis for the expression of "self" and "belongings to self.
The other [types of ignorance] are different from that.

Just as there are eight types of beings including Māra, so too is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) the eighth. Furthermore, false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is established among these as the fifth. Or, it is the basis for acquisition (*āyakṣetana*), consisting of the eyes and so forth belonging to one's own and others' continuums (*svaparasāntānika*), because of the statement, "consisting of the twelve bases. [It refers to] objects such as form (*rūpa*).

Ignorance arising from the continuum of the five sense-faculties is [the ignorance] regarding the internal; or rather, it is that which is distinguished by speech and so forth due to prior tradition. "Knowledge regarding the internal and external" refers to the knowledge of selflessness as if there were no distinction between one's own and another's continuum for one who does not discern it. And this is a unique, undifferentiated ignorance.

(95) Regarding "ignorance with respect to karma": it is that ignorance which arises from doubt concerning the existence of merit and demerit; or, it is the ignorance of those who deny the existence of merit and demerit. This very [ignorance] is called "ignorance with respect to karma. The distinction is that in the former case it is associated with doubt, whereas in the second case it is associated with false conviction (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). [Regarding] maturation (*vipāka*)—

"What is ignorance (*ajñāna*)? It is to be explained as before: [it consists of] doubt regarding the existence of maturation (*vipāka*), and the views of those who claim there is a means to pacify that [doubt]. Ignorance regarding the maturation of karma means [ignorance] concerning both karma and its maturation. It is the lack of knowledge regarding the designations (*saṃprajñapti*) such as "Lord" (*Īśvara*) held by the Tīrthikas. That very [ignorance], when conjoined with long duration and extreme intensity, is called "undifferentiated" (*aviśeṣaka*). [It is also] the perception of a cause and effect where there is no cause. [106]
Having said this: "This very ignorance is stated as being one and the same; for by means of it, they remain utterly deluded even regarding the ripening [of karma].

Therefore, it is because of the non-performance of the cause, or because of the house and so forth belonging to those who do not know the cause. For he who does not perceive the cause does not understand that the ripening is preceded by a cause. Consequently, because of his false view, he has not conquered what was not yet enjoyed, and thus he is favored by enjoyment."
It is touched upon.
This very cause, characterized by action (*karman*), is described through the distinctions of "well-performed" and so forth, for the purpose of grasping the clarity of its various types.
In the case of well-performed action, it is characterized by the ten paths of wholesome action; in the case of ill-performed action, it is characterized by the ten paths of unwholesome action.

Regarding "good and evil deeds," this refers to the manifestation of mental aspirations as taught in the scriptures, which consist of the various modes of engagement with sentient beings characterized by the paths of wholesome and unwholesome karma. In the same way, for those who possess doubt or those who profess [a particular] reality, that lack of knowledge regarding the truth—whether it be doubt, wrong view, or ignorance concerning good deeds and so forth—is called "ignorance regarding the object. It is called "ignorance regarding the cause" in relation to the maturation [of karma].

Regarding "ignorance with respect to cause and effect": this refers either to ignorance regarding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), or to the ignorance concerning houses and so forth which lack a [true] cause. Furthermore, one who perceives no cause cannot admit that even the ripening fruit is preceded by a cause. Therefore, ignorance associated with false causes is said to be characterized by the non-continuity of cause and effect.

Ignorance regarding cause and fruit is to be understood precisely as falsity with respect to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in their various transformations; it is precisely as having the nature of being accompanied by causes. Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) exists as the sequence of cause and fruit to be investigated, because it is "originated" (*samutpanna*) in the sense that it has come forth (*sam-ut-pad*) in dependence.
"By virtue of having the nature of dependent origination" means that what is conformable to its fruit is "dependently originated.
And by establishing it in this way, both [the cause and the fruit] are subsumed, because they lack any independent existence as cause and fruit.
And this being so, it is not like the occurrence of cause and effect,
or like that of father and son. Thus,

whether one is engaged in practice, has attained certainty, or has not yet begun, whatever ignorance they possess is respectively called "ignorance associated with the path," "ignorance associated with certainty," or "ignorance associated with false causes."
"Lack of knowledge regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha" means:

lack of faith, or lack of certainty, or non-engagement [in practice] with respect to the Buddhas, the well-expounded nature of the Dharma, and the excellent practice of the Saṅgha, respectively—whether through ignorance, as previously described.

"Lack of knowledge regarding suffering" means: having heard that the characteristics of suffering, its origin, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self are such, the subsequent awakening [to them], and so forth, as previously described.

"Ignorance regarding origination" means that, as before, having heard of the characteristics of origination—namely, the characteristic of cause and the characteristic of condition of the origination of origination. "Ignorance regarding cessation" means that, as before, having heard of the characteristics of cessation—namely, the characteristics of cessation, peace, excellence, and renunciation of the cessation of cessation.

"Ignorance regarding the path" means that, as before, having heard of the characteristics of the truth of the path—namely, the characteristics of being the path, the right method, the practice, and the realization.
"Non-knowledge regarding the wholesome and the unwholesome" refers to the factors conducive to awakening along with their opposites.
In this context, the factors conducive to awakening are the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the meditative concentrations, and the limbs of awakening.
Their opposites are non-knowledge, laziness, restlessness, forgetfulness, distraction, and lack of clear comprehension; these fourteen states are to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
Those factors conducive to awakening are wholesome;
among them, those which are such are wholesome, while their opposites are unwholesome. [109]
The accumulation of those [actions], or the arising of their consequences, whether through deliberate intent or through denial, is as previously described. Regarding "faulty and faultless":

the faulty are the objects of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) as they have been explained. For instance, the killing of living beings is called "faulty" because it obstructs the wholesome; and that [obstruction] is the cause for these [unwholesome states]. Therefore, they are faulty. Regarding "in these"—[the text continues with the discussion of] these [faulty states].

They are irreproachable. They are precisely those factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*), because they are the essential core. Regarding "those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated": those very factors conducive to awakening are called "to be cultivated" by virtue of being the cause for repeatedly bringing them into manifestation. For one repeatedly cultivates the cause—

They are called "great" because they are so; these sense objects (*viṣaya*) are not to be cultivated because, being unwholesome, they do not deserve cultivation. Those [ordinary] objects are inferior because they are exhausted by the purpose of merely nourishing body and mind. The factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*) are sublime because they serve the purpose of nourishing body and mind. For indeed, those factors conducive to awakening are like a field for one who is concentrated and whose vigor is uninterrupted.
And they bring about the state of being an effect. The dark [factors] are associated with the seat of suffering because, being faulty, they do not lead to liberation.

The bright factors, which are the wings of enlightenment, lead to that liberation because they have that as their purpose. For the mind and volition are indeed the basis for those [factors], and there is a ripening of them within those [states]. [110]
Alternatively, it is the lack of knowledge as it truly is regarding the spheres of contact (*sparśāyatana*) and the four gates, which constitutes this specific type of misconception.
This ignorance (*avidyā*) should be understood as the primary factor in the process of progression, beginning with the thirty-six [factors] on the side of cessation (*nivṛtti*).

Furthermore, that which is the cause of progression for the progression—such as the exertion of movement here, which is connected to one's own awakening—and likewise the thirty-six [factors] consisting of the causal basis for the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma; [This is the intended meaning of the passage.]
Those who have taken refuge in the ethical discipline that is the basis for cessation;

or rather, those who have realized both the self and what belongs to the self as being non-self; furthermore, from the perspective of the object of meditation, there are the twelve sense bases and dependent origination.
That which is present is the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*).
Those which are obstacles are their opposites (*vipakṣa*).

That which is the intrinsic nature is the engagement in the bases of contact according to the settling of attachment; I see this as the side of cessation (*nivṛttipakṣa*), by way of being the antidote to the view of existence (*sakkāya-dṛṣṭi*)—from the point of the non-connection with consciousness up to its exhaustion.

For what purpose are [terms] such as "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) and "non-seeing" (*adarśana*) explained with their full elaboration? It is for the sake of someone whose mind is of such a nature, so that they may hear the meaning of those things prescribed for that time in their proper sequence. Through that very designation, [the intention is that] there might be no crookedness (*avakra*) on his part; many such purposes are stated because of the nature of the recitation of the mantras.
Now, it was stated in the *Abhisamaya* that all modes of conduct involving impurity are designated as unwholesome (*apathya*).
It is said that absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) is to be personally realized, and that there is the conduct of those who are incapable [of such realization].
Apart from everything that is to be practiced, one should point out the manifestation of the true nature (*tattva*) as it has been thus attained; it is not a matter of verbal exposition.
The subject matter is that which is to be explained;
it has been stated along with its purpose and the factors conducive to its practice.
(Formations: 2)

He states that which is to be designated, that which is to be explained, and that which is to be pointed out as the formative forces (*saṃskāra*): "The formative forces are the sacrifices and so forth. What are the formative forces?
A question arises from the presence of doubt;
for this term *saṃskāra* is intended to denote all conditioned phenomena, as in the statement, "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.
Yet it is also used for a single part of them, as in the expression, "one should perform a consecration (*saṃskāra*)."
It is also conscious.
"What is the aggregate of the appropriation of formations? It is precisely these six groups."
Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as well, it is said: "the formative forces of life (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) are the formative forces of longevity (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*).
There is the commencement of their collective arising;
however, it is not made known what the underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) here is.

Regarding that, he states the threefold basis: "the formative forces (saṃskāras) are not [directly] cognized. He further states that even these are not made known: "the formative forces of body, speech, and mind.

Here, by means of distinctions, the Blessed One has described the differentiation of the formative forces according to the divisions of body and so forth; however, he did not state their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

Alternatively, the question "What are the bodily formations? is asked for the purpose of stating their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). He replies: "They are those associated with non-discernment" (*asamprajñātāḥ*). [Objection: But surely, in this context, the Blessed One previously provided a teaching on the intrinsic nature and only afterwards gave a teaching on the distinctions?
For example: "What is feeling? It is experience. And that [experience] is "pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
However, in this case, the definition of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is given after first providing a detailed classification (*prabhedanirdeśa*).
There is no fault here, as both [the classification and the definition] are presented in that manner due to the requirements of the context.
Therefore it is said:
"Many words and deeds of manifold forms have been employed by you here and there, according to the differences in the dispositions of those to be trained."
"Inhalations and exhalations.
Why? He says: "Because they are conditioned by the body, like the movement of a saw," and so forth.
Thus, because they are produced by the body through a mind bound to it.

Because they function as the basis for superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the body and have that superimposition as their cause, they "construct" the body; thus, the bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*) are called "superimpositions" (*adhyāsa*). This becomes clear in the heart. He speaks of the vocal formations (*vāksaṃskāra*): "The vocal formations are [the thought] 'I have spoken'. He says:

"Having reflected upon the desire to speak, one utters speech. And: "In such and such a way I shall speak"—thus [it is]. Having explained the vocal formations, he concludes: "The reflection upon the desire to speak."
This being so, it should be understood that there is no difference in the formative activity (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*) of speech.
He states the formative activities of the mind: "the volition of one whose mind is impassioned," and so forth;
this refers to the volition of one who is impassioned, which is conjoined with attachment (*rāga*).
Thus, the volition of one who is hostile is associated with hatred;
the volition of one who is deluded is associated with delusion.
Concluding the discussion on the mental formations (*manaḥ-saṃskāra*), he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
And here, the inclusion of volition associated with passion and so forth is for the purpose of including wholesome [volitions] by way of implication;
otherwise, wholesome volition and the like would not be included under the category of "formations" (*saṃskāra*),
and thus there would follow the consequence of contradicting another Smṛti.
And this is not accepted.
Therefore, it should be explained as "for the sake of the object by means of application.
Thus, it should be understood that [the mind] is for the purpose of further mental formation and for the purpose of further conditioning.
To this it is replied: there, the specific actions of body, speech, and mind belonging to the devotees (bhāgavatas) were called "formative forces of the body and so forth" (kāyādi-saṃskāra);
here, however, the formative forces of the body and so forth refer to the superimposition (adhyāsa) and its cessation.

In this context, are specific types of karma intended, or are only the [four] applications (adhyāsa) and so forth meant? Both are intended. Regarding the applications and so forth: the non-distraction from the body and other [objects] is called "application" (saṃskāra).
In another passage, specific types of karma are mentioned for the purpose of further conditioning.
How is this known?
From both scripture (*sūtra*) and reasoning (*yukti*).

For it was said by the Blessed One, the Kūrmayogin, to me: "That *saṃskāra* overpowers even meritorious *saṃskāras*, and even non-meritorious ones; it overcomes even the *saṃskāras* of peace, being composed of ignorance.
And those who possess knowledge of merit and demerit do not rejoice when they are directly confronted by the senses, because of the possession of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
And the great elements are unceasing and uncreated.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Furthermore, it has been stated—"Among the various types of merit, through the non-consummation of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), there arises a consciousness that destroys the merit; thus it continues until the attainment of final knowledge. This consciousness of the formative force has been described in this way. Therefore, it is determined that while consciousness approaches the formative force, it is the formative force itself that projects [the result].

Furthermore, it is said: "Having conditioned the bodily formations for one’s own self, up to [conditioning them] for the world perceived as a sentient being. And in this context, non-connection (*asaṃśleṣatā*) is not the cause for what is heard. This is because it has been stated that there is no production of a single identity (*naikātmya*) inherent in the great elements (*mahābhūta*), and so forth. Moreover, those things described as "non-produced," etc., lack the capacity for maturation (*vipāka*) and so on, as seen in the previous counter-example (*vipakṣadṛṣṭānta*). If this is so, how can those bodily formations be considered "auditory"? They are so designated because they arise from a distinct application (*viviktayoga*) such as "conditioned by the body," and so forth. Furthermore, even the intended speech is referred to here as "conditioned" (*abhisaṃskṛta*) by way of its being a seal of speech (*vākyamudrā*); thus, those two [bodily and vocal formations] alone are indicated, but not the conventions of speech (*vākyasamaya*). As for mental formation (*manaḥsaṃskāra*), let it be as one desires; it is not contradictory.
It is asked: why are the formations of body and so forth, characterized as karma, taught in such a sūtra? It is said: it is with regard to specific disciples present [at that time].

For, without the teaching here of the formations of body and so forth—which are characterized by specific types of karma—they would otherwise understand those formations of body and so forth, characterized as karma, through their own personal experience alone.
This was not stated even with regard to those disciples who lack self-awareness;
for it is held that they attain realization of reality only through teachings that are concordant with their own disposition.
This is because the teaching is given in a single manner.
There is also a logical argument:
conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are accepted as being the condition for consciousness (*vijñāna*).

If both intention (*āśaya*) and exertion (*samudghāta*) were admitted to be bodily formations, then due to their connection with intention and exertion, there would not be a mere condition consisting of what is conceptualized by both.
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is indeterminate, unteachable, obstructed, or characterized by the intention to destroy or uplift, to serve as the condition for consciousness,
because it lacks association with the knowledge that has turned away from conceptual proliferation.
Therefore, the formative forces of body and so forth are intended to be specific types of bodily and other actions characterized by merit and the like.
The characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) has been explained.
[117] It was stated that there are "six groups of consciousness" (*ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya*);
in this regard, the Blessed One has described the differentiation of consciousness according to the distinct substances of the eye and so forth, but not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is merely a partial indication, depending on specific distinctions of time;
for indeed, even the distinction of the sixfold cognition has not been stated here—
this has been stated only as a general outline.

"Skilled in the groups of consciousness. By this term "group" (*kāya*), the differentiation in the functioning of the visual consciousness and the others with respect to external objects such as form is also shown;
for it is by means of the distinction between the cognition of blue and other [colors] that the visual consciousness and the others are established as having external objects.

Otherwise, there would be only six consciousnesses, as there would be no purpose for the word "body" (kāya). Having observed that it is established merely by way of number, and not by way of specific designation, he says: "visual consciousness up to mental consciousness."

Now, why was it not also stated in the detailed exposition—from "the group of visual consciousness" up to "the group of mental consciousness"? To this it is replied: because here [in the verse], the meaning of the term *vijñānakāya* has been described as "arising from a cause that is not audible," and because the word *kāya* signifies a collection (*samūha*) of consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).

Furthermore, why is it that this—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—is not mentioned in the Sūtra? To this, the answer is: "Eye-consciousness is the discernment of form based upon the eye. Since the consciousnesses of the ear and so forth are understood through the same principle (*vyadharmeti*), they should be known here in the same way. Moreover, the discernment of the self is conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra-pratyaya*), according to the statement: "That consciousness which has not yet reached its desired course."
In successive births, it arises as a continuous recognition in due order.
Regarding mindfulness as well, it is said: "And that which they call consciousness, Ānanda, one should not, by any means, allow that city to be joined with desire.
[The phrase] "they do not exist" follows.

And here, "consciousness" (vijñāna) is intended as mental consciousness (manovijñāna), because it is described thus: "One who has been born in the intermediate state (antarābhava) between death and rebirth possesses only mental consciousness. However, in this context, the distinction regarding consciousness is established by consciousness itself.
It has been stated that there are six groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*).
Since discernment (*pratisaṃvijñāna*) occurs by means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), how could there not be a contradiction? There is no contradiction.
For the Blessed One has analyzed consciousness in its entirety within the *Sūtra* by way of its unreal application;
however, regarding consciousness as conditioned by formations, it should be understood according to what is possible.

Just as name (*nāman*) was explained in detail in the context of the specific differentiation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): "What is form? Whatever is form, all that consists of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements"—thus has the entirety of form been analyzed.
But when name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is established with consciousness (*vijñāna*) as its condition, it is established according to how it occurs. Thus it is said.

Therefore, for that which has consciousness as its form, no designation by means of words—whether primary (nirdeśa) or secondary (lākṣaṇika)—is intended; nor is it [designated] by secondary words as being itself. According to the Sautrāntika view, this results in a direct contradiction.

Because for that [being] who has passed beyond formative forces (*saṃskāra*), the six groups of consciousness are intended as the consciousness of the formative forces themselves, and not merely the consciousness of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi-vijñāna*); such is the explanation regarding the nature of consciousness.
(5. Name-and-form):
Having explained the portion consisting of consciousness, he states the portion consisting of name-and-form: "Name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
Thus it is said that name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
Furthermore, this word "name" (nāma) is used in the sense of a designation even when it is dissociated [from the object], as in the case of the four Vedas and the aggregates (skandhas).
Therefore, the objection raised there is irrelevant.

To refute [the view that these are] dissociated [from mind], he says: "The sense organs, such as the eye, [arise] from forms. According to the Sautrāntika school, internal form is the non-manifestation (avijñapti) of external entities;
however, according to the Vaibhāṣika school, because it is dissociated [from mind], it is internal form as a conditioned factor (saṃskāra).
And all of this, in the pair [of name-and-form], is intended as "name" conditioned by consciousness, not merely as a designation.

This is because [otherwise] there would be the futility of the self. Feeling (*vedanā*) consists of pleasure, pain, and that which is neither. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the grasping of signs. Following that, the mental factors (*caitasika*), tranquility, and non-definitive knowledge constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
When these aggregates are made objects by consciousness, they are called "name. Why? Because they are like salt water.

The meaning is that it is "name" (*nāma*) because it undergoes transformation through the process of cutting off craving and so forth at its beginning and middle; or, it is "name" because it bends toward other births, such as the womb and so on; or, according to another interpretation, it is "name" because it inclines toward substances such as form (*rūpa*), since it grasps the characteristics of a child's body.
In the *Pravacana*, it is stated that there are both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derivative elements (*bhautika*).
Therefore, having stated that "form is great in its power," he says "whatever form there is.

By this designation, "whatever form there is," it is shown that there is no form distinct from the primary elements (bhūta) and their derivatives (bhautika). The term "derived" (upādāya) means "caused by [the primary elements]."

Just as it is understood that that which is not determined by way of grasping is thus without cause, so too, by the phrase "not grasping the great elements," it is understood that the great elements are made into causes. These five aggregates—in the form of the *kalala*, *arbuda*, *ghana*, *peśī*, *śākhā*, *mahāśākhā*, and so forth, consisting of the extremely gross pentad—are the accumulation of consciousness, which becomes the manifestation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). They are called "elements" (*bhūta*). He asks: "What are the elements made into? and replies: "Namely, the earth element," and so on. This section on the elements is for the purpose of describing their color, location, shape, arising, and transformation, because they possess distinct individual characteristics and general characteristics.
The element: the wind element performs the function of supporting the body and so forth; the great elements such as skin and so on [are included]; not three.

He does not see it. It is as futile as the leg of a bedstead because it cannot be grasped. Because its own nature is not understood, he asks: "I am making myself a vessel for questions. He says: "That which is heaviness. Taking up what is called heaviness within the category of derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*), there is no comprehension of it; thus he says: "It is like a suit of armor. "Hard" means solid. "Light" refers to the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*) characterized by lightness. Because it exists in conjunction with heat and moisture, the nature of the wind element is declared to be for the purpose of movement. If that which is light and of the nature of motion were not the wind element, [it would not function as such].

"But that derived form (*upādāyarūpa*) of his is indeed swift. This indicates that this form and the preceding name are condensed into a single unity; thus, it shows that both have a single referent. Now, one might object: "Since it is not observed that for those who have attained rebirth (*upapatti*), name-and-form arises solely with name-and-form as its condition, how then can it be said to have them as its condition? It is replied: We have not investigated the mere recollection of names belonging to their own species as being the cause of this.

Rather, the state of being a condition for other distinct and specific objects of perception has been examined. Otherwise, one would have to speak of an unexamined examination-condition, such that consciousness were the condition for consciousness. [123] Having explained name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), he speaks of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): "The six sense-bases have name-and-form as their condition," and so forth.
It has been stated that the six sense-bases have name-and-form as their condition.
In that regard, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are twofold:
external and internal.
Therefore, in order to exclude the external ones, he says: "the six internal sense bases," and so forth.
The term *āyatana* must be explained.

Now, since from the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) onwards there is a convergence of the body and mind bases with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), why is it said that the six bases have name-and-form as their condition?
It would rather have to be said that the four bases have that [name-and-form] as their condition.
Let it be so;
however, it has been stated that they fall within the scope of the application of hearing the scriptures (*śāstra-śravaṇa-praṇidhi*).
Those sentient beings who possess the eye and other faculties based upon the body have their bodily basis fully complete.

At that time, the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) becomes complete by way of its support (*āśraya*). It is said to be "complete" because it is comprised of the six consciousnesses and because its supporting condition (*āśrayapratyaya*) is fully present;
the meaning is that there is a complete conjunction of all its supports.
The six sense bases have been explained.

Immediately following this, contact (*sparśa*) is to be explained; thus he says: "Contact is that which arises from the six sense bases"—thus it is said that contact is [defined by] the six sense bases.
Contact (*sparśa*) also functions as a nourishment; it is observed even when there is contact, and here too, association (*saṃgati*) is mental (*caitasika*).
Therefore, the sequence is not fixed, such that one would say "the six sense bases" followed by "contact. Contact is [simply] contact.
Regarding this, the *Triṣvāṇa-śāstra* says: "There are six groups of contact (*sparśakāya*).
Even though there is a further division, six are clearly perceived.
It says: "eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact."

And here, the Blessed One has stated the classification of contact (*sparśa*) by way of the sense-bases such as the eye, but not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is because it is designated by the term "contact" only in dependence upon a specific determination of its basis. What, then, is the intrinsic nature of contact? It is stated in the *Aṣṭavakra*: "Whatever constitutes the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), or the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), all these are dependent upon contact."
But surely, here [the mind] is not perceived as a distinct entity like feeling and so forth.
How, then, is it to be understood? Like the eye and other [faculties], it is known through the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Just as: "What is the eye? It is the basis of visual consciousness, the clarity of form."
Nor is the moment of perception delimited;
for even though it is interrupted by the five groups of consciousness, it is nevertheless followed by one's own vision.
It is just like that. [125]

Is it not true that its intrinsic nature has already been stated by the Blessed One? For it is said: "Dependent upon many forms, visual consciousness arises; the coming together, the conjunction, and the meeting of these three is contact."
This is a metaphorical designation of the effect upon the cause, just as "Buddha" is used [for the Dharma]. However,
for one for whom there is contact from the coming together [of the three], the resolution regarding the meaning of "contact" is as follows.
However, it should be understood that for one for whom contact (*sparśa*) is precisely the coming together (*sannipāta*), its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has been indicated here by the statement:
"from eye-contact up to mind-contact.
In this context, all five—the visual faculty, the auditory faculty, and so forth—are called contacts associated with the path of practice (*pratipat-sparśa*).

"Contact through mental engagement (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) is contact with designations (*adhivacanasaṃsparśa*). Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) operates upon objects by transcending [the range of] ordinary people, whereas there is no such entry for the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*). It is called "designation" (*vacana*) because it is speech; contact associated with that is "contact through mental engagement. The first [type of contact] is characterized by its basis (*āśraya*), while the second is characterized by its association (*saṃprayoga*). Contact has thus been explained.

(Feeling—7) Feeling must be explained. Regarding that which is associated with it, he says: "One feels by means of contact as its basis. Thus, contact is said to be the condition for this feeling. And feeling is of three kinds. Which feeling has contact as its condition?

Intending this, he says: "The six groups of feeling. Which six? He says: "Born of eye-contact, born of ear-contact," and so forth. By this, only the classification of feeling—determined by the specific circumstances at that time—is shown; it is not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For its intrinsic nature is one. This has been explained.

Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The coming together of these three is contact (*sannipāta*). From that, feeling (*vedanā*) is born; this is feeling born of eye-contact. And it is of three kinds: pleasant (*sukha*), which is agreeable (*sāta*); [and so forth].
The meaning is that it is "beneficial" (*anugrāhikā*) to the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
The meaning is that "suffering" (*duḥkha*) is that which harms the sense faculties and the primary elements.
Furthermore, "neither-suffering-nor-pleasure" (*aduḥkhāsukhā*) is the opposite of both of these.
In this way, there is the conjunction of all three as well.
That which is born from mental contact is "pleasure";
immediately following that moment, it is "mental joy," the army of Brahmā's bliss.
It is called "suffering" because it is a moment of mental distress (*daurmanasya*).
If applied thought (*vitarka*) is a feeling (*vedanā*), then that which was said by the Blessed One in another Sūtra—"Whatever is felt here, all that is suffering"—is to be understood accordingly;
thus, there is no contradiction.
The sequence [of the teaching] is based on a specific intention (*abhiprāya*).
What is the intention here?
"O Ānanda, having in mind conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) themselves and their objects, I have said: 'Whatever is felt, that herein is included within suffering.'"
It is also said in a verse:
"Having understood the impermanence of conditioned formations as well as their subject to change, the Fully Awakened One, the Knower, declared that feeling is suffering. [128]
Thus, the intended meaning has been shown in the Bhagavadveda.
Therefore, since there is no inherent suffering in the two types of feeling pertaining to the two doors and their sub-doors, it is shown that their suffering is intentional (abhiprāyika).
Feeling has been explained.
He says that craving is the flow toward what is worthy of feeling—namely, "craving has feeling as its condition.
It has been stated that craving has feeling as its condition;
and that [craving] is of six kinds according to the distinction of its bases.
Furthermore, [craving] is threefold according to the distinction of body and so forth within the six sense-doors;
it is sixfold again according to the distinction of its objects.
Therefore, how can craving not have feeling as its condition?
Thus he said: "If [they are] the groups of craving.

Here too, the Blessed One has stated the divisions of craving according to the distinctions manifested by objects such as form and so forth, but not its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), with regard to the specific objects.

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all [the afflictions] is characterized by attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*), just like a desirable object. Attachment, moreover, is a form of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); it is the repeated engagement of the mental continuum (*cittasantati*) with objects such as form (*rūpa*).
Such engagement is not possible without attachment, because it is absent in those who have abandoned craving.

If craving has feeling as its condition, then since everyone possesses feeling, it might be suspected that they would all necessarily fall into the state of having craving. To address this, he asks: "How so?
Just as rain is said to have [clouds] as its condition, does it follow that whenever those [clouds] exist, rain must necessarily occur?
Is it not by means of bulls? Even so, although sensations exist, craving does not necessarily arise.
Why? Because [the teaching] provides the antidote.
Indeed, through a specific antidote, the suffering of craving comes to an end; otherwise, even when afflicted by sensations, nirvāṇa would not be possible.
Just as even in conditioned things like milk and water, there is no arising of sprouts of *nirvāṇa* and so forth;
and the Blessed One has declared the self to be contradictory [to this process]: "Dependent upon feeling born of contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśaja-vedita*), craving arises.

Because of the absence of that [feeling] when there is an absence of feeling born of contact with ignorance, and because one who possesses the antidote does not have such a nature, therefore craving is not logically established as dualistic.
In that case, why was it not contradicted there as well—namely, the statement: "Craving has as its condition the feeling born of contact associated with ignorance"?
For it has been made known that ignorance serves as the general condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and because it has the same purpose [as the specific conditions].

If craving has feeling as its condition, for what reason is ignorance stated in some places as the non-specific condition for craving—as in: "Monks, ignorance is the cause of craving, ignorance is the condition for craving, ignorance is the source of craving"?

In some places, contact (*sparśa*) is also stated [as a condition for craving], as in: "The sixth contact is craving. But here, it is stated that feeling (*vedanā*) is the condition. How could there not be a contradiction? There would be no contradiction, because it is merely a matter of connection. For ignorance (*avidyā*) is the general condition that brings about craving, and contact is also [such a condition]. This is because [ignorance is the cause] of all cravings within the realms (*dhātu*)—[130]
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the common cause for the various afflictions (*kleśa*), such as the ground, the course, and friendship; thus, ignorance functions as the instigator, as it is said:
"The fault of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) has ignorance as its cause.
Contact (*sparśa*) likewise is certainly a factor in the general category of craving.
Therefore, all these are equally included in the [formula]: "The six [types of] craving born from contact with the eye and so forth.
Thus, it is stated that contact is the cause of craving;
furthermore, feeling is stated as the specific cause, having been intended [by the Buddha].

Thus, it should be understood that for craving belonging to the desire realm (*kāmabhūmikā*), only feeling belonging to the desire realm is the cause; for craving belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna, only feeling belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna is the cause.

In this way, for the higher stages as well, by taking into account the specific causes of the distinctions in craving—such as the distinctions in wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth—it is understood that this "feeling" was mentioned in the summary verse as the cause for the distinctions in craving.
Thus, craving has been explained. [131]

And the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) constitute the clinging to sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*). The adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) constitutes the clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavratopādāna*). [This refers to] the view that the self is supported by the body, or that the body is supported by the self. Vows (*vrata*) consist of the practice of asceticism and the undertaking of various bodily observances.
The restraint of body, speech, and mindfulness is within the two arms.
[133] Why is this gift that wards off cold and bestows satisfaction joined separately from the *iṣṭis*? It is said:

because of the heart-space of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. This is because the attainment of liberation is demonstrated through the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Vijñāna; [and] the offspring of the back...

Those who desire to grasp [the truth], having their minds distracted by false paths, have been deceived even by this [system] through [the teaching of] non-existence and so forth, despite its being designated as "one's own path.

Even though it has been set in motion here, it is understood as a purification through the transformation of the objects of this world. By this, [it is shown that] what is not spoken of [as such] is the destruction of cold, produced from the *tasṛṭṭī* [or *tatsṛṣṭi*]. [137]
The attachment, pride, and so forth that have form as their object and range within the [desire] realm, as well as doubt and the rest, are indeed to be abandoned by vision;
these are called "clinging" (upādāna) because they are the root of clinging.
Appropriation has been explained.
(Bhava—10) Having explained clinging (*upādāna*), he speaks while pointing out the limb of existence (*bhava*): "Existence has clinging as its condition"; such is the sequence of existence.

It has been stated that "existence (bhava) has clinging (upādāna) as its condition," and it has been specified that this very existence consists of the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandha).
In another place, however, it is stated that there is only one [entity], and its divisions are merely intended [conceptually].
Therefore, since it is not known what is meant by "existence" (*bhava*) here, he says: "Existence is the *caitya*."
And what are the "bases" (caitya)? They are:
"existence in the desire realm" (kāmabhava), and so forth.
Existence associated with the desire realm is "existence in the desire realm."

Through the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopa*), as in the case of *marīcigānaka*, it means: "one who is associated with form (*rūpa-pratisaṃyukta*)," "one who is associated with the object (*ālamba-pratisaṃyukta*)," or "one who practices form and mind as objects according to their respective application. This refers specifically to the "passion for sensual desires" (*kāma-pramada*) in its conventional sense, and not to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, in order to explain its intrinsic nature, he asks: "What is the passion for sensual desires? He explains: "There are eight hot hells. There are also cold hells; they are not mentioned here because the intention was to list them in their specific order.

The cold hells, however, will be described later. In this regard, a *naraka* is so called because beings are led (*nīryate*) there and experience the perception of non-merit. "Saṃjīva" and so forth: that place where winds revive (*saṃjīvayanti*) sentient beings who have been killed is Saṃjīva. Therein are the black threads (*kālasūtra*).

Sentient beings are variegated by their falling; it is said that at that time they follow after it. Where the mountains are pervaded on both sides by clouds, and sentient beings are oppressed, that is sorrow.
Where sentient beings are being protected, there is supreme joy and independence.
That is *raudra* (the fierce);
where it is especially so, that is *mahāraudra* (the extremely fierce),
wherein there is equality with fire and the other elements.
That [hell] is Tapana;
however, where there is a particular intensity, it is Pratāpana.
There, by means of the five fires of affliction, such as excessive cooking and so forth—
For those beings, the jewel of the bliss of awakening is a gift spread with a fierce fire. Furthermore, what are these? They are the half-dvika, the *hṛthādi*, and so forth.
For those beings who are half-enemies (*ardhadrohmānām*), boils and pustules arise from cold as a cause of distress.

In the absence of agitation, those who are exceedingly proud of their own physical strength produce sound with their tongues through the specific quality of coldness. [139] Through the application of great growth, even from the tongue, it is produced by the internal stalk behind the palate.
Due to the appearance of characteristics such as eyes like blue lotuses and so forth, an excess of flesh arises on the body;
therefore, because it is a transformation of the word "Kāśyapa," this [state] is indeed the path of the past. Thus, they are called "pretas."
They are called *pretas* because they have departed (*ita*) from this world without returning;
or they are called *pretas* because they are like *piśācas*;
or they are called *pretas* because their movement is extremely swift (*tivegamana*).
"In the sacred teaching (pravacana), it is said: 'By one who has abandoned the mind, there is no grasping'; whereas in common worldly usage, it is said: 'The gods are the city-fortress.
[140] "The gods are the city-fortress."
"Beginning with Dīrgha" refers to the divine beings. "The Cāturmahārājika [gods]" refers to the four great kings who are world-protectors: Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Vaiśravaṇa.
Among them are the Cāturmahārājikas;
the meaning is that they are situated in their midst.
Likewise, for the sake of rebirth in that very place, one must dwell among the gods; this is the meaning.
Those who exist in the abode of the Four Great Kings are the Cāturmahārājikas;
they reside in the white cities of the four directions from the middle world.
"Naṣaṭtriṃśāḥ" means those who are reborn in those [realms] through their karmas together with the fourteen gods and the *ahaṃkāra*. Thus they are called "Naṣaṭtriṃśāḥ."
Furthermore, there are eight Vasus, twelve Ādityas, eleven Rudras, and twelve Ādityas;
thus it has been stated. Because this is experienced in that manner, worldly people say "thirty-six. And in accordance with that, such is the conventional usage in the sacred teachings (pravacana).
Regarding the Yāmas:

they are called Yāmas because they have gone (*yātāḥ*) to your back (*pṛṣṭha*). Each and every Yāma [is so called] because it extends (*tanoti*) the great day (*sro hula-mahaḥ*) and the great night (*hula-micamudrātraḥ*). Regarding the Tuṣitas: by means of *tuṣa*...

The Tuṣitas are so called because they are endowed with contentment (*tuṣṭi*) as their offering; or alternatively, they are the Tuṣitas because they are fully satisfied (*tuṣāḥ pūrṇāḥ*) by that very designation. Regarding the Nirmāṇaratis: these are the Nirmāṇaratis because they take delight (*rati*) in the creation (*nirmāṇa*) of enjoyments (*bhoga*) produced by themselves. Regarding the Paranirmitavaśavartins: these are those whose nature is to exercise mastery (*vaśavartin*) over enjoyments created by others.

[The gods] who wield power over the creations of others (*paranirmitavaśavartin*); likewise, [the gods] belonging to the Brahma-realm (*brahmakāyika*). In that regard, he is called "Brahmā" because he is produced from roots of merit that are free from malice (*adruhuka*). Who is he? He who is endowed with the great vows (*mahāvratasaṃyukta*), has attained the intermediate meditative absorption (*dhyānāntara*), and subsequently abides as the lord of the fourth [meditation].

Because of their existence: since they dwell there together with the previous ones, they are to be understood as the Brahmakāyikas (the Retinue of Brahmā). As for the Brahmapurohitas (Ministers of Brahmā):
they are called Brahmapurohitas because they are placed before (puraḥ) Brahmā.
Regarding "the Mahābrahmās":

those who are distinguished by specific excellence in lifespan, complexion, sovereignty, and supernatural power are the Mahābrahmās. Regarding "the Parīttābhas": their light is limited, being situated within the protection of the heavens; thus they are the Parīttābhas (Limited Light).
Nābhāsas, Prabhāṇas, Nābhāprabhāṇas, Prabhānupetas, and Apraprabhāṇābhas.
[143] "Sukha" is said to mean "pure" (*śubha*). Because they are pervaded by that which is self-delighting, they are called Parīttaśubhas ("Limited Purity").

"Aśrāṇām śubhabhogam" means those who possess auspicious enjoyments despite being inauspicious; "hṛstena śubhabhogam" means those who have auspicious hands that perform auspicious deeds. That wealth which is not acquired through deceit is the happiness of others as taught in other scriptures. "Abhraveśām" refers to those who have no connection with the earth (the clouds), hence they are called *unabhrakāḥ*; for it is said: "Even now, their pride regarding that [earth] has not ceased along with their existence. This is because they are sustained by the karma of the *ānirjika* [or *ānirjika*].

Because there is the dissolution (*pralaya*) of these merits, they are called "those for whom merit is dissolved" (*puṇyapralayāḥ*). Because their fruit is vast (*bṛhat*), being like a provision for the journey (*pātheyanikam*) that brings about a great result in another place, they are called "those of vast fruit" (*bṛhatphalāḥ*). Regarding "without sound" (*anudrāḥ*): according to the view that it refers to those who remain as long as the *uṣṇīṣa* [is present], they are associated with the abode of the Śūdras (*śūdrāvāsa-yutāḥ*). [The term] *śūdra* refers to the non-Aryans among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

"Śūdrāvāsāḥ" means those whose dwelling place is among Śūdras. Even for one who is a lord in a Śūdra-dwelling, [the term] "ukkhuṣṭīlāva-vṛttitā" refers to those who are not noble (anūrāḥ). Or, because they abandon their state of being through destruction or time, they are called "abuddhe" (those who have lost their intellect).
Those who cause distress through superior confidence and arrogance are those lacking in skillful means (*anupāya*).
Those who are satisfied with a mere semblance of pure non-duality are extremely corrupt. Those who are deluded by the words of illustrious non-dualists are the foolish.
These are the best among these types; they are established in the highest nature.

[Regarding] the sphere of infinite space and so forth: at the time of the preparatory application for meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), because it has the aspect of space, it is a derivative of space. Its very non-cognition is that [attainment]. By this very [non-cognition], there is the cognition of non-cognition.

"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to that very non-perception [of objects] because at the time of the preparatory stage for meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it has that as its mental aspect (*ākāra*). "Nothing exists" refers to that very non-perception because at the time of the preparatory stage for meditative attainment, during mental attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth, it has that as its mental aspect. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is a boil, perception is a thorn, and even the eye is delusion; thus, there is only the cessation of the festival of perception. This is the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called "existence" (*bhava*) in the context of the truths regarding debt and taking.

And here, karma—which is like a worm in the mud of future doubt—is expressed by the word "sūtra. By this very "existence-sūtra," it is further stated that "this is rebirth"; just as [the name] Vṛhaspati is derived from *vṛha*. And it is said in another sūtra: "That which is arising... [140]
Furthermore, regarding that which brings about rebirth based on desire, it is said: "And this [existence] as 'becoming' (*bhava*)," and so forth in detail.
It was stated by way of sequence:

"What is existence in the realm of desire (*kāmabhava*)? It is that karma associated with the realm of desire, conditioned by grasping (*upādāna*), which brings about [rebirth] in the future," and so forth in detail.
"What is existence in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*)? It is that karma which is associated with the realm of form," and so forth.
"What is existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*)? It is that karma which is associated with the formless realm," and so forth.
Therefore, it is karma itself—functioning as the fruit in the future—that is intended here as the specific distinction [of existence] according to the divisions of desire and so on.
The explanation of the place of rebirth is indeed for the purpose of showing this very sequence of rebirth.

If "existence" (*bhava*) here were merely "karma," what would be the distinction between that and the "formative forces" (*saṃskāras*)? The distinction between the two is that karma which is immediately past is a formative force, while karma which is immediately present is existence. Thus, the limb of existence has been explained.

Having thus explained *bhava* (existence), he speaks while pointing out *jāti* (birth): "Birth has existence as its condition. This refers to those various [beings] who are distinguished by the specific types of existence resulting from their respective latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Regarding this, it is said: "In all classes of beings (*nikāya*)."
Whatever constitutes the inclusion of anything— such as the inclusion of all things beginning with the gods—
is called "birth" (*jāti*) and "origination" (*sañjāti*). These synonymous terms are uttered for the purpose of showing specific states.
For one who has trained accordingly, there occurs the arising of sensation from name-and-form and so forth.

For that which has been born, there is the full development of name, which is "birth. Just as in the world, one whose five [faculties] are fully developed is said to be a "born being," so too, for one whose name-and-form is complete, there is "rebirth" here in a specific state of the body.

The transition of consciousness (*saṃkrānti*) is the state of the remaining faculties once [the being] has been reborn. The manifestation (*nirvṛtti*) of one who has entered the womb and is emerging from the mother’s field—characterized by the attainment of specific excellence—is the functioning based on causal conditions (*nimittavṛtti*).

The emergence (*prādurbhāva*) is the contact with the birth canal and the state of existence following birth. Knowing it thus, one fully understands birth. This is the definition of the distinctions between the stages of birth (*jāti*).
[479] The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) consists of the various perceptions (*saṃjñā*) through the differences in form, genus, and taste.
He shows the apprehension of a self through the words "the acquisition of the aggregates" and so forth;
for in this way, there is a threefold apprehension of a self regarding perceptions.

Even the attachment to the notion of a self within the perception of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth arises from the conceptualization of the three types of faculties; it is the grasping at the aggregates and so on, thinking:
"I am one," "I am the embodied one," and "I am the enjoyer of objects."

For the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is the differentiation of a heap; thus, by grasping it as an aggregate, one falls into the error of imagining [the self] as something other than what is desired.

By understanding that "element" (*dhātu*) is merely phenomena (*dharma*) based on its etymological derivation, the grasping of it as an element avoids the error of imagining it as having spatial extension.
The eyes and so forth are the "bases" (*āyatana*) because they are the gateways for the apprehension of objects.
In the phrase "kuvidurūpīti āyatane," the inclusion of the term *āyatana* (sense-base) is for the purpose of excluding [the sense-bases] such as the riverbank (*nadītaṭa*) from the conceptualization.

Having thus explained the characteristic of the genus (*jātilakṣaṇa*) in detail according to the distinctions of states, he explains it again in brief: "by means of the aggregates, bases, and elements" is the mark (*liṅga*), and the state of being an object of apprehension for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
In this way, the characteristic of the genus of perceptions (*saṃjñā*) belonging to persons (*pudgala*) who possess the cognition of what is to be experienced has been stated. [140]

In that regard, "newly arisen" refers to the fresh production of cessation (*nivṛtti*). When the two *jau* [syllables] have ceased, it is that which is capable of being accompanied by the existence of this prior state of being for sentient beings who are superior; thus, it has ceased within that homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
It is distinguished by the substances that have arisen from formative forces (*saṃskāra*);
and that [arising] is said to be distinguished by duration (*sthiti*) and birth (*jāti*).
Briefly stated, the condition for rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*) within a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) is called "conjunction" (*samabandha*).

It is indeed reasonable that, among the fivefold genus (*jāti*), the first genus is the cognition of difference. But how is it said that [the first] is the cognition of the subsequent member in a *tatpuruṣa* compound?
For, by means of its occurrence, it is like that in the first genus.
Capacity is imparted [to it].

Because it proceeds toward that which is characterized by the non-arising of the fivefold pentad in five locations, it is called "conditioned by that" (*tat-pratyaya*) due to its being the primary cause.
The genus has been explained.
(Old age and death—12):
"With the destruction of birth, there is old age and death.
And as it has been stated, the detailed exposition occurs.
Therefore, for the purpose of explaining old age (*jarā*), he asks: "What is old age?

It is seen as characterized by the transformation of the physical form through sixteen terms in detail, beginning with "grayness" (*śālikya*) and "whiteness of hair" (*pālitya*), which signify its state of decay.

It is characterized by the transformation of the material body (*rūpa-vipariṇāma-lakṣaṇā*), and the destruction of the hair is mentioned; the destruction of the hair is what is called "baldness" (*khālitya*).

Regarding the deficiency of the hair: as it is said—"Grayness" refers to the deterioration characterized by the transformation of form due to the deficiency of the hair; this deterioration is struck down by the process of transformation, and that transformation is called old age (*jarā*).
But how is the destruction of the hair itself old age?
It is said:
because the destruction of hair is not distinct from that [transformation];
for there is no destruction of hair without transformation.
"From the contraction of one's own light"; as it is said: "the abundance of power.
Without the contraction of one's own light, there is no abundance of power. "From the weariness of falling away"; as it is said: "withered."

The depletion of flesh and blood: as it says, "it withers," meaning the face becomes parched. Regarding the distortion of the body's configuration: as it says, "having the form of a hunchback or a curved roof-rafter."
The rafter is the wood that supports all the timber of the gabled chamber;
it is curved like a wooden ladle,
and by means of it, the body comes into being.
[The text reads: "Of Gopāla, [there is] the ridge-pole and the rafters. [It continues:
"By the ornament of the *tilaka*, the portion of the face is marked.

In the state of old age (*bāḍhkeva-avasthā*), the body becomes pale and covered with *tilakas*; this is heard as the constant sign of the transformation of strength (*balavipariṇāma*). As it is said: "Like a field, like a sword, like a cloud, like a fading [color]."
In the state of non-abiding, one falls and becomes deluded.

As it is said: "In front, there is the state of prior non-existence. Regarding the state of movement, it is said: "Like a staff, there is a crooked bending, characterized by the transformation of wisdom, which exhausts the moving body in its perception," as it says: "It bears the burden of the Dharma."

Since there is a distinction between the dharmas leading to happy rebirths, which are blameless, and the non-dharmas leading to miserable rebirths, which are blameworthy, it is possible to know the goad of speech. Endowed with the differentiation of the basis (*āśrayabheda*), he demonstrates the transformation of mindfulness characterized by the cessation of the non-dual nature of this [mind] through the destruction of its seeds; thus he says: "It arises now."
He speaks of "the destruction of the book" (*pustakopaghāta*) to demonstrate the characteristic transformation of sexual intercourse and impurity; he says, "decline" (*hāni*).
The destruction of the book is the decline of those things that are consumed through sexual enjoyment and the belly.
He speaks of "diminution" (*parihāṇi*) to demonstrate the characteristic transformation of food, drink, and enjoyment within the stomach, occurring through the state of being consecrated by mantras.

Since the nature of change has been explained in due order as being characterized by decay following acquisition and existence, he now describes the impermanence of the conditioned (*saṃskāra*) through its exhaustion: "The decline of the faculties" refers to the exhaustion of the formative forces of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) by the casting off of their continuity, which is a summary of the transformation of vitality; thus he says, "the state of antiquity of the formative forces.
Because they lack stability and are subject to impairment, he says, "the state of decrepitude."
The non-clinging to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
It has been made a refuge (*saraṇa*), thinking "I am here. That which is called "bursting" by this [term], and so forth, are the ten synonyms explained in detail.
In that regard, because it does not deviate from its accumulation (*sañcika*), there is a clear manifestation (*sphuṭi*) that is indistinguishable from the continuum (*tantrikāya*).
For it indeed ceases at the end of death;
that cessation is the "ceasing" (*skhavana*).
That immortality is to be fled from, since one who is dissimilar falls away.
For that which is unimpaired and nameless, its differentiation consists in the coloring of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and so forth.
Of what nature is it said to be?
It is that which has not yet abandoned its wind, smoke, and fire, and which is of a single form characterized by non-satiety and cleansing.

When there is the cutting off and disappearance of the faculties of form and so forth, such as the eye and others, it is completely cut off in every respect because it is no longer a fire. Having thus shown the twofold grasping of the causes for its persistence in due order, he says: "the loss of life-span; the loss of heat."
Upagupta anticipates this with the words "and the preparation of food"; thus, by these two, the distinction of the final door is shown.

The mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) of the two entities and their passing away (*cyuti*) have been indicated. By two [verses] the fullness, by two the lack of form, and by two the mutual dependence and the state of passing away have been demonstrated. For in this way, Upagupta, having exhausted [his merit], [attains] that gradual passing away and that state of passing away.

Both of these are designated as "death. Furthermore, when one whose vital energies (*upaga*) remain partially intact dies suddenly, there occurs the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), just as life itself is the cessation of death. It is the cessation of one's own karmas through the possession of the life-faculty; as it is said—"through the cessation of one's own karmas. Thus, by all means, it is designated as death.

What, then, is the cessation of the life-faculty? He says: it is the passing away (kālakriyā). And the meaning is that it is the non-distinction of the previously mentioned wind-constituents (vāyu-saṃskāra). Thus, the limb of old age and death has been explained. [116]

Immediately after dependent origination, there is the recitation of the truths; and as it was announced, so it is explained. Desiring to explain them, he sets them forth: "In that regard, what are the four noble truths?"
These are truths for the noble ones; therefore, they should be understood as "the Noble Truths.
Are these not truths for others?
For all beings, these are truths because they are non-erroneous reality.
However, for the Noble Ones (āryas), these [truths] are as they are;
