they are not perceived in this way even at this [present] time. Therefore, these are called "truths" because they are not deceptive, and not because they are non-deceptive through a distorted vision.
Those intent on that [the Beyond] declare the two gateways to be happiness; those who know the truth beyond them perceive them as suffering.
That which those beyond [the gateways] declare to be happiness, those below perceive as suffering.
Thus by the words of the verse.
But why is this sequence of the truths—from suffering up to the path—as it is? It is said:
whichever truth is realized first, that one is taught first.
The sequence of exposition follows the order of realization (*abhisamaya*).
Why is it that realization pertains only to the truths? It is said:
Since one who is attached to suffering is afflicted by suffering, and from suffering one falls into delusion—it is precisely this that is examined here.
Subsequently, [one considers] "What is its cause? and thus reaches the origin (*samudaya*); thereafter, [one considers] "What is its cessation? and thus reaches the cessation (*nirodha*).

Then, [thinking] "What is the path for this?", he seeks the path. Illness, its diagnosis by one who knows it, the subsequent application of treatment, and the eradication through the power of knowledge—these very points provide the illustration for the Truths. How so? "A physician who has arrived at the connection through four factors... [160]
For six days he becomes a king, he becomes worthy of kingship, and he is counted among kings.
By which four? He is skilled in his own wheel, skilled in the exertion for his own wheel, skilled in the maintenance of his own wheel, and skilled in the excellence of his own wheel.
In the same way, by these four factors, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Unsurpassed One, instructs the monks with the designation "six days."
What are the four? Here, a monk understands as it really is: "I am a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha"; he understands as it really is: "This is the noble truth of suffering";
he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering," "This is the cessation of suffering," and "This is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
(The Truth of Suffering—1)
"Birth is suffering" refers to the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
"Old age is suffering" refers to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
"Sickness is suffering" refers to the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
"Sorrow" is easy to understand.
In brief, these very aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) are suffering, because they include the flood of suffering pertaining to the fruit.
But is it not the case that only a portion of feeling (*vedanā*) is suffering?
How is it that all five aggregates of clinging are called suffering?

Because of the three types of suffering—the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*). Due to their association with these [three], all the aggregates, when they have an object of perception, are said to be suffering.

Since pleasure also exists, why is it that only suffering is designated [as the truth]? Because of the pervasive nature of suffering. It is like calling a heap of filth "a collection of jewels" even when one has fled far from a few difficult places. For what wise person would designate the mere scraping of an itch with a ragged cloth as "pleasure"? Thus, it has been said that suffering is all-pervasive.

(Regarding *samudravasuyam*—2) Desiring to explain the state of being the ocean (*samudraya*), he introduces [the topic] with the words: "having made the ocean of suffering its fish. They call suffering the "ocean" (*samudra*); it is called an "ocean" because one wails (*rud*) there excessively on all sides. Although it is the cause of suffering, it is called the "ocean of suffering" (*duḥkhasamudraya*). The detailed explanation is: "craving for rebirth, which is delight accompanied by passion. Rebirth means plunging into a new birth. That which connects one to that [rebirth] is "pertaining to rebirth" (*ponarbhavika*).

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is a certain degree of delight (*nandī*) or mental gladness (*saumanasya*). Attachment (*rāga*), however, is well known as having the characteristic of affliction (*saṃkleśa*). Through its differentiation, it leads to connection with renewed existence (*punarbhava*); for instance, one prays, "May I be," rather than "May I be a god or a human," O Bhaisajyaraja—that is craving for rebirth (*paunarbhavikī tṛṣṇā*). And because it conceals the true nature of the manifestation of the self and its enjoyments, it is called delight-attachment (*nandī-rāga*). Due to its pervasive activity and its quality of forming a continuous stream, it is said to be associated with that delight-attachment.
And here the word "saha" (with) has the sense of identity;
the meaning is that joy rests upon other forms of passion,
just as [in the phrase] "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*maitrīsahagata*) refers to descending into the factor of enlightenment that is satisfaction (*tṛpti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Just as in the phrase, "cultivating the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness accompanied by loving-kindness," it is understood that there is an association with loving-kindness; for since mindfulness as a factor of enlightenment cannot coexist with those [states] as its direct companions, there is a connection through auxiliary factors.
Likewise, here too, one should see the connection between craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and passion (*rāga*) as being through auxiliary factors, because they are considered to be in opposition.
Furthermore, delight-and-passion (*nandīrāga*) is the cause of craving.
Furthermore, because it is the cause of renewed existence, it is said to be associated with delight and passion (*nandīrāga-saṃprayukta*). In this context,
it is called "rejoicing" (*abhinandanī*) because its meaning consists in the impossibility of conceiving of [the cessation of] objects and enjoyments.

Furthermore, the purpose of renewed existence through differentiation is stated as a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), just as the supplementary part [of the Vedic passage] says, "May I be a god, or a human. Therefore, in this case, even this sequential enumeration by the Blessed One is connected with the summary enumeration. And how, and in what manner, is craving [the cause]? It is the cause of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) when there is doubt regarding non-cessation; [it is the cause] of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as desire and so forth.

Because it is the state of being a cause; and the cause is the origin (*samudaya*). Furthermore, it has been said: "Monks, suppose there are five kinds of seeds—unbroken, unrotted, undamaged by wind or sun, not deprived of their husks, and lying comfortably on the earth—and there is the earth element, the water element, and the fire element. In this way, those seeds reach growth, sprouting, and abundance. Monks, this is a simile made for the purpose of making [the meaning] understood. This illustrative meaning should be seen as follows: "The five kinds of seeds" is a metaphorical expression for consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*) in its state of accumulation. "The earth element" refers to the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Only these three possess the nature of the three factors:
the seed is the cause, the teacher is the condition, and that which is accompanied by the collection is the origin.
The stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*) are also the cause of establishment.

Since it would be established by the ocean-like number of causes for the non-severance of the sequence and for the production [of existence], why is the ocean-like number of causes for thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) mentioned separately here?
Among those worthy of offerings,
he has approached the one who possesses the primary cause for being an object of veneration.
Thus [166].
For this karma, when conjoined with craving, is capable of producing the sprout of renewed existence, whereas karma alone is not;
because the underlying intention (*āśaya*) is the cause of renewed existence, the cessation of craving—which persists as long as the root exists—is assisted by the cessation of craving itself.
Furthermore, ignorance (*avidyā*) and karma are the common causes, since there can be no latent tendency (*anuśaya*) devoid of delusion (*moha*).

Likewise, even if the twelve factors of dependent origination are not present in their entirety due to detachment (*vairāgya*), they are nonetheless incapable of preventing rebirth because the three [factors] to be experienced in a future existence do not exist;
this is because of the absence of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). For this very reason it has been said: "The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are the root of existence."
The Saṃyuktasūtra has been quoted.
(3. The Concomitant of Cessation) Immediately following that, he speaks of the Truth of Cessation: "What is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering?
The cessation of suffering is the "cessation of suffering" (*duḥkhanirodha*).
The teaching of the Śiṣṭas is that there is no abandonment of anything in reality;
thus, there is the "remoteness" and so forth of that very craving.
Therefore, when false views have been abandoned and ceased right here, the [stages] proceed up to the unsurpassed knowledge of exhaustion.

"Throwing out" (*kṣepa*) is the instruction. Why? Because it is seen as the abandonment of all that causes agitation. Having stated that all things which cause agitation must be dispelled, he says: "complete relinquishment" (*pratiniḥsarga*).
"Removal" (*vinodana*) refers to the casting away of the afflictions through the state of aversion toward their re-arising;
it also has the sense of "obstructing," as when it is said: "the state of being brought to an end."
The "obstructing" refers to the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so forth.
"Vanishing" (*vyantībhāva*) means the state of being gone (*vyabhāva*). And the meaning of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is what he expresses by the word "destruction" (*kṣaya*).
Because of the abandonment of those things to be abandoned by vision through the means of those [factors] to be abandoned by cultivation;
and because it has the sense of the path of cultivation, as he said— "detachment" (*virāga*)—
which is the complete exhaustion of passion and the rest.
And the meaning of the path without remainder is what he calls "cessation" (*nirodha*),
because of the abandonment [of defilements] without exception and without possibility of recurrence. And that which abides in the removal of obscurations is what he calls "attainment" (*cyupagama*).
Due to the disappearance of the obscuration that is not contradictory [to liberation], there is the attainment of supreme liberation.
When he said, "The non-arising [of defilements]" while seated in the Upeṣī celestial palace,
there would be no such vision even during his visit to Pukkusāti, because that was the most excellent dwelling.
Others, however, explain some of these words in a different sense.
In every creation, at the time of each new beginning, all things proceed in regular succession; thus, "prati-vi-sarga" means emergence.

It is made clear by the qualifying term as "ending with *pra*. Since non-existence (*abhāva*) results from the cessation (*vyasana*) of existence, "vyadyana" means non-existence, which signifies the state of emergence [from that cessation].

Cessation (*nirodha*) is the abandonment of the entity characterized by the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*). It is called "cessation" because all afflictions and all calamities have been specifically expelled and have reached a state of non-existence. This is the non-arising of all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, due to their being eternally non-existent.
"Thus, those states that are to be abandoned—such as hatred for the Teacher, hatred for the Dharma, and hatred for the Saṅgha—are to be relinquished," according to the Sūtra.
Both the brief statement (*uddesa*) and the detailed explanation (*niddesa*) are exactly as before.
Furthermore, it has been shown that both aversion toward the Teacher and aversion toward the heart [of the teaching] are to be directed toward Nirvāṇa.
The reality of cessation has been explained.
Immediately following that is the reality of the path (*mārgasatya*).
He states its referent as follows: "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering," and so forth.
The cessation of suffering is the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanirodha*), which is *nirvāṇa*.
That going toward it is the "excellent path" for attainment; thus, it is the noble eightfold path, the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
For the path itself is called the "practice" (*pratipad*), because it leads to the realization of *nirvāṇa*.
"The noble chariot," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
"Noble" refers to one who is not ignoble.
"Path" refers to the path undertaken by one possessing the essence (*somin*) for the sake of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding how the sixfold group is [defined], he says: namely, from right view up to right concentration.
Having entered [the path], the unshakable way has been shown.
Because they constitute the path of hearing, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are the sequence of hearing.
Right concentration and right mindfulness are the aggregate of concentration.
Because it serves as the means for transcending saṃsāra, mindfulness is called the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*).
For it is said that when mindfulness is established, the mind is concentrated by being freed from distraction.
Right view, right resolve, and right effort constitute the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*).

Volitional effort (*saṃkalpa-vyāyāma*) is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of wisdom (*prajñā*); however, because it is capable of expressing that [wisdom] and is directly conducive to its realization, it is spoken of as such. Thus, the four Noble Truths have been explained. [116]
Immediately after the Ārṣeya-saṃsthā, the faculties (indriyas) were mentioned; he now asks: "Which are the twelve faculties?
They are called *indriyas* because they exercise sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) over their respective objects.
This is explained in detail as "the eye-faculty," and so forth. [The text continues with] the ear-faculty, the eye-faculty... [and so on].

The objects of the faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the body are each their own respective [spheres] (*āyatana*). Furthermore, the object of the mind is all things (*sarvārtha*). In the case of femininity, it is the female faculty (*strīndriya*); in the case of masculinity, it is the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*).
In the maintenance of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), it is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); and in perception, it is the five feelings (*vedanā*).
For it is said: "Attachment underlies pleasant [feeling], aversion underlies painful [feeling], and ignorance underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling].

This applies to the five [faculties]. For instance, as stated in the *Vaiśeṣika-karma-nirmita*: "In some cases they exert themselves; the paths conducive to penetration are excluded from the factors of the path. Regarding the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing, there is the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*). Regarding the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation...

Abandonment is the relinquishing of the faculty [of sensation]. This is the relinquishing of the faculty of one who dwells well in the wholesome dharma, and the relinquishing of the state of experiencing the fruit of liberation.
In that regard, the faculties such as the eye arise in the desire realm and the form realm, but not in the formless realms.
In that regard, because of the absence of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and because those [faculties] do not exist in the form realm,
the two faculties of female and male exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). However,
the two faculties of mind and life exist there as well, since they are present even in the form realm.
In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) consists of what is felt as associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness.
The faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) is felt in the mental clarity of Rāma. For Rāma, the thief of desire, there is said to be a feeling characterized by these two arrows.
There is bodily suffering and mental distress.

Because of the statement "bodily suffering," this refers to pleasant feeling associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), as well as the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) associated with the three groups of sensory consciousness in the first *dhyāna*.
Mental pleasant feeling in the third dhyāna is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Mental pleasant feeling in the desire realm, as well as in the first and second dhyānas, is the faculty of mental joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
Neutral feeling—neither painful nor pleasant—whether physical or mental, is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), because it is free from conceptualization (*avikalpaka*).
That exists in all three realms.
How is this known?
Because there is another [feeling] distinct from pleasure and pain.
(21b) There is a third experience, according to the Sūtra; the commentary is likewise.
For it is said in the Sūtra: "The wise one knows feelings: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant."

Furthermore, it is said: "For one who is greedy and intensely greedy, and for one who experiences great suffering, that which is neither painful nor pleasant is called the basis of equanimity. Thus it is stated.
There is also its functional activity (*vṛtti*).
It is understood to exist because it arises from a representation (*vijñapti*) devoid of feeling (*vedanā*), and because it is perceived as being experienced and endured.
The five [faculties] beginning with faith exist in all three realms, except for those whose roots have been severed.
Among them, faith is the clarity of the mind;
vigor is enthusiasm for wholesome objects.

Memory is that which follows upon the experience [of an object]; it does not arise from the very moment of that [original] production, for the cognition of the word has already perished by the time the feeling is experienced in the interim. That is the "indifferent" (*upekṣin*) cognition. What is the essential nature of this?

Furthermore, what is the reason that this is formulated as being associated with something else? [This is a different opinion. Concentration (*samādhi*) has a single basis; wisdom (*prajñā*) is the discernment of phenomena (*dharmavicaya*).

The initial power of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), which has entered the state of being cultivated with respect to its object, is what is called "vision" (*darśana*). As for those nine factors— the five beginning with equanimity (*upekṣā*), faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth, along with mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)— which constitute the "aspects" (*ākāra*), when they rely upon the state of being untainted (*anāsravatva*), they are established as the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

It is explained. What is the reason? The path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) consists of four untainted (*anāsrava*) paths; it is understood that [this process] begins with six [moments] in the stage of the candidate (*āgāmin*). For that person, the faculty is one whose greatness and enjoyment have not yet been fully mastered.
"Nine" refers to the form of turning away after having excluded another eon; however, nine substantial entities (*dravya*) do not occur within a single eon.

Having removed [the faculties] through pleasure and mental joy, one will indeed act according to the state [of the mind]. For if that path belongs to the stages of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), or the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), or the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), then there is only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) therein, not the faculties of pleasure or mental joy.
If it belongs to the stages of the first or second dhyāna, then there is only the faculty of mental joy (*saumanasyendriya*) therein.

The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is not weak there; rather, in that [third dhyāna], there is only the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and not a weak faculty of suffering. And it is precisely these nine faculties—the mental faculty (*manaindriya*) and the others—that are called "faculties" on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

They are established [as such]. What is the reason? In the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is no contradiction with the formless [attainments]. However, that very same person realizes the four truths for the sake of abandoning the remaining qualities of cultivation and so forth. Therefore, the faculties of that person are not withdrawn. [108]

Those same nine faculties in the path of no-more-learning (aśeṣamārga) are established as the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya). What is the reason? In the path of no-more-learning, the mind that desires what is already known is "perfect understanding" (avabodha).

That [state] also exists as the "faculty of having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), which either transcends the faculty of having known (*ājñātendriya*) or possesses the nature of being free from the exhaustion of what remains to be known. Likewise, there are the faculties of one who has become thus: the faculty of having known and the faculty of one who has known.
In this very context, they are also included through the application of the wholesome and through equanimity alone.
Just as these self-meditations (ātma-dhyāna) have the faculties of space, consciousness, and nothingness (vijñānākiṃcanya-bhūmika) as their respective faculties, so too do the beings born there.
Now, for those belonging to the first and second stages, the faculty of mental pleasure (somanasyendriya) is present there;
and for those belonging to the third and fourth stages, it is known that the faculty of the bliss of existence (bhava-sukhendriya) is present.
"The faculties have been explained.

[116] Immediately after the faculties, the meditative absorptions (dhyānas) are discussed. Regarding this, he says: "In that regard, what are the meditative absorptions? They are the practices performed therein.
Now, what is the meaning of "these are meditations" (*dhyānāni*)? It is *dhyāna* because one meditates by means of it;
that is, in the sense of knowing through wisdom (*prajñā*), due to the knowledge applied as appropriate by one whose mind is concentrated.
Alternatively, this verbal root has the sense of reflecting (*cintana*).
And "thought" (cintā) is established as the definitive conclusion (siddhānta).
This is what is meant: meditative absorption (dhyāna) is one-pointedness of a wholesome mind; it is synonymous with concentration (samādhi).
Pointing out the first dhyāna, he says: "In this regard, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual desires...

This refers to concentration (samādhi), which is designated as "freedom from passion for sensual desires" because it enters into that which is contrary to sensual desires. To show that it is not a minor state, he says: "secluded from sensual desires."
It is secluded from desires— that is,

from the latent tendencies (anuśaya) belonging to the desire realm, such as passion and so forth— and it is secluded from evil, unwholesome states (dharma), for the purpose of fulfilling the literal meaning [of "secluded"]. [160]
"With applied thought (savitarka) and with sustained thought (savicāra)" means it exists together with applied thought and together with sustained thought.
"Born of seclusion" (vivekaja) means born from seclusion;
what is this so-called seclusion? It is the stage of grasping the fivefold knowledge.
Furthermore, among the dharmas of the dhyānas, the pure [dhyāna] appears as "joy and bliss" (*prītisukha*). Both joy and bliss constitute "joy and bliss.
Joy is mental ease (*saumanasya*).
Bliss is the bliss of pliancy, characterized by constant adaptability.
One should inquire about this so as to attain concentration;
"the elephant in rut" indicates the fivefold meditative attainments.

By this, the attainment of the first dhyāna is said to be endowed with five factors (*aṅga*). The five factors are: seclusion (*viveka*), investigation (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and concentration (*samādhi*).
Since the term "dhyāna" is used, "concentration" is thereby expressed.
In this context, by the word "pleasure" (*sukha*), "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*) is indicated.

Why is there an association with volition (*cetanā*)? For at the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), temporal pleasure is not tenable, because the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) are absent;
nor is mental pleasure tenable, because of the mention of "joy" (*prīti*).
Joy (*prīti*) is mental ease (*saumanasya*).
Furthermore, there is no simultaneity between pleasure (*sukha*) and mental ease (*saumanasya*), as they have different objects of focus (*ālambana*).

Nor is there a conjunction with the five [mental factors] of the first dhyāna, because their occurrence has been observed [to be distinct], and because of the mention of "five factors" (*pañcāṅga*). [163]
He describes the attainment of the second dhyāna with the words beginning "he, in solitude," and so forth.
"He" refers to the yogi.
"The state of being desired in four ways" [refers to the following].

Because the attainment of the second dhyāna is satisfied by the very experience of tranquility, which is free from the agitation caused by the impact of seclusion and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*).
It is described as "inner clarity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) and so forth. What, then, is this so-called "inner clarity"?

It is the clarity born of faith (*śraddhā-saṃprasāda*). Because for that yogin, following the attainment of the second dhyāna, there arises a turning away from the agitation of "I am" (*asmi-māna*), it is called "internal clarity" (*adhyātma-saṃprasāda*); for it is due to the one-pointedness of the mind (*cetas-ekotībhāva*) that this occurs.
The term "one" (*eka*) implies non-diffusion.
The movement of what has been made.
"One" and "end" (koti) form "one-end" (ekoti). The state of being one-end is "the state of being one-end" (ekoṭībhāva).
These objects are directly the single destination of the mind;
because from the second dhyāna upwards, mindfulness is held to be absent and meditative absorption is devoid of its constituent factors.
Therefore it says: "In the third [dhyāna], there is one-pointedness of mind and equanimity;
joy and bliss," as before.
Thus, the attainment of the second dhyāna has been shown as being endowed with its constituent factors (aṅga).
There are four factors: joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*), and internal clarity (*adhyātmasamprasāda*).
Demonstrating the attainment of the third dhyāna, he says: "From detachment from joy," and so forth.
Since the attainment of the third dhyāna is intended to be indicated by the term "mental ease" (*saumanasya*), he therefore says: "From detachment from joy."

"He dwells in equanimity" (upekṣako viharati): here, it is equanimity regarding mental formations (saṃskāropekṣā) that is intended—characterized by non-exertion toward joy—and not equanimity as feeling (vedanopekṣā) or immeasurable equanimity (apramāṇopekṣā), because those two are excluded here. "Mindful" (smṛtaḥ): [this refers to mindfulness].

Equanimity-concentration is mindfulness; clear comprehension is wisdom. The phrase "mindfulness and so forth, and happiness with the body" indicates that it pertains to the mental body, because one experiences mental happiness and not physical, for one is indeed equanimous.

Because the state of completion (*samāptatva*) is absent in the *Pañcaviṃśatikā*. Here he states an illustration: "That which consists of substance is the scripture and the aphorism. The Noble Blessed One is such because of his abandonment of mastery over the realm of desire (*kāma*). The etymological derivation (*nirukti*) is: he has gone far away (*ārāt yātaḥ*) from evil deeds, and he is worthy of being honored even by those nearby; thus he is called "Ārya. The meaning regarding the disease (*roga*) has already been explained. And the reality (*tattva*) is in the third place.

The completion [of the path] is said to consist of five factors. The five factors are: equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), independent movement, and mental action (*manaskarma*). If it is argued that this refers to mental action, what is the benefit of there being five seals (*mudrā*)? Furthermore, in the teaching on the fourth dhyāna, there is no mention of "purity" (*śuddha*). If it is argued that purity refers to a continuity (*prabandhi*) conducive to pure sensation (*vedanā*), then [this would apply] to the third [dhyāna].

Why is there a continuous connection (*prabandhi*) with the appropriation (*upādāna*)? If it is argued that this is because it has been impaired by equanimity (*upekṣā*), we say no; for equanimity itself is for the sake of increasing that [appropriation]. This is because it is distinguished as having purity as its effect. As it is said: "Among dharmas, at the time of the occasion, the one who possesses the two-fold purpose of the meaning is the cause of purity; desiring the destruction [of defilements], he directly demonstrates the non-perverted [truth]. When the root of mindfulness is present, the continuity of those who have abandoned dryness is indeed dryness.

If it is asked how the functioning of the *samāsa* (the latent deposit) is to be understood: it is because it produces its effect through the suppression of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), or by means of a continuous stream of a single pure-feeling (*śuddhavedanīya*) [karman], or due to a specific distinction [in its nature]. If it is argued that it is known as "meditative absorption" because of its similarity [to it], we say no; for even under the influence of meditative absorption, there is pleasure and equanimity.

In the fourth [chapter], he speaks of the attainment of dhyāna: "of pleasure and of wisdom," and so forth. Regarding pleasure, there is one verse; regarding suffering, there are two verses. For, upon the very acquisition of the first dhyāna, there is the disappearance of that which is to be experienced as suffering. Upon the acquisition of the second dhyāna, there is the disappearance of physical pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*). Upon the acquisition of the third dhyāna, there is the disappearance of mental joy (*saumanasya*).

Therefore, it says: "Of pleasure and wisdom," and so forth. This is because there are two kinds of bodily [feeling] to be established within the experience of pleasure and pain, and two kinds of mental [feeling] to be established (namely, joy and dejection). Regarding "neither-pain-nor-pleasure": this refers to the feeling characterized as neither-pain-nor-pleasure, which is mentioned in connection with the attainment of the fourth dhyāna; for in that attainment, there is the enjoyment of pleasure and the other [feelings], yet the nature of that attainment is devoid of [ordinary] feeling.

By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), feeling (*vedanā*) must possess the characteristics as previously described. Regarding the phrase "purified by equanimity and mindfulness" (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddham*): the meaning is that it is purified by equanimity and purified by mindfulness. Here, a compound is possible. Furthermore, by the word "equanimity," one should understand the equanimity of mental formations (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*), not the immeasurable equanimity (*apramāṇa-upekṣā*), because the latter is inappropriate here.
It should be understood that the purification of equanimity is indeed manifest through the departure from the three types of unease (*ayoga-kṣema*).
And those eight factors are: vitarka, vicāra, joy (prīti), and the fourfold group beginning with bliss (sukha).

Thus, in the attainment of the fourth dhyāna, there are four factors: neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (aduḥkhāsukhavedanā), purity of equanimity (upekṣāpariśuddhi), purity of mindfulness (smṛtipariśuddhi), and purity of concentration (samādhipariśuddhi).
For what purpose are these established within the dhyānas, among those specific factors, and in such a distinct sequential order? Why are no other contacts (spraṣṭavyas) mentioned?
That is explained as follows:
concentration of the self (*ātmasamādhi*) consists of the antidotes to initial thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and their application.
Among these, in the first dhyāna, it consists of the antidotes to initial thought and sustained thought.
In that [first dhyāna], there is the antidote to the discursive thoughts of sensual desire, ill-will, and cruelty;
and joy and bliss constitute its benefit.
In the second [dhyāna], because the opposing factors have been countered by the noble state free from discursive thought and investigation, one attains the bliss of seclusion.
The desire for seclusion has as its nature the reliance upon both of those [the body and the mind]. Its function is the restriction of seclusion by virtue of that reliance.
In the second dhyāna, internal serenity has as its nature the counteragent.
Because it is the antidote to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*),
and because joy and bliss (*prīti-sukha*) constitute its benefit;
the desire for seclusion is as described before.
In the third dhyāna, equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension constitute its nature as an antidote,
because they serve as the antidotes to joy;
bliss constitutes its nature as a benefit.
The desire for discernment (*vivekakāmatā*) is as previously described.
In the fourth dhyāna, the purity of equanimity (*upekṣā-pariśuddhi*) and the purity of mindfulness (*smṛti-pariśuddhi*) constitute the nature of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-ātman*),
because these serve as the antidotes to pleasure within the dhyānas.
The neutral feeling (aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā) has the nature of being a benefit;
the desire for seclusion (viveka-kāmatā) has the nature of being the basis for both of those.

[116] Just as one who is connected to the realm of desire (kāma-pratisaṃyukta) attains knowledge connected to the realm of form (rūpa-pratisaṃyukta), so too does one who is connected to the realm of form and is to be assisted attain knowledge connected to the realm of the nameable (ākhyeya-pratisaṃyukta); thus he says: "for all, the perception of form (rūpa-saṃjñā) and so forth."
Because of the distinction of gross form, all [beings] possess desire for it;
however, even there, form certainly exists.
In that regard:

Because it is stated in the Sūtra [190]: "The non-sounding of the elements (dhātus) is to be declared," there is no form (rūpa) therein, like a tree. Therefore, this is called "omniscience" (sarvajña) because it is non-different from and superior to the knowledge of all things.
It is the knowledge of each thing; that is, the knowledge of each individual entity or according to each state. That [knowledge] belongs to the one possessing form (rūpin).

It arises from the mutual exclusion [of objects]. It would be like entering into a perception of pure form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*). Because it is limited by the measure of form itself, there is no perception of various objects (*nānālambana-saṃjñā*). Because it is limited by space, there is no perception of various forms (*nānākāra-saṃjñā*), nor is it a lack of mental attention (*amanaskāra*). At the time of practice, for yogins who abide in the infinite aspects, this is taught as liberation: "space."

He dwells having attained and entered the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Desiring to transcend the sphere of infinite space and so forth, he grasps the sign from the completely purified bodies of consciousness;
thus, by focusing on "consciousness is infinite," he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

However, through equanimity (*upekṣā*), there is the accomplishment of the resolve (*abhimokṣa*) regarding the perception of detachment from that; therefore, he says: "There is nothing whatsoever," and so forth.
"There is nothing whatsoever" refers to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*).
Because there, due to the perception of infinite forms by the mind of a monk, they abide in the state of "nothingness" (ākiñcanya) in an incomparable manner.
Now,
through the application of the manifestation of perception and from the gateway of non-perception, [one attains] the body purified of perception.
Because perception is subtle,
it is not that perception is absent there, as is the case with things such as a dewdrop.
Nor are there two designations [for them], as in the case of the three stages called "meditations" (*dhyāna*);
for they are indeed designated from among humans, yet they enter into that state as if being non-designated.
And immediately after this, it is said: the four divine abodes (*brāhmavihāra*) have been taught.
To explain them, he asks: "What are the four divine abodes (brāhmavihāra)? He provides the answer: "In this case, monks, a monk... [and so on] "...accompanied by loving-kindness (maitrī)."

Supreme loving-kindness (*maitrī*), however, is the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the welfare and happiness [of beings]; for loving-kindness arises when one attends to the thought, "O, may sentient beings be happy!
Loving-kindness is its defining characteristic.
A mind associated with that is "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*maitrīsahagata*). By means of that [mind], [one practices].
It should be understood that the purpose of the connection between the seven phrases is to counteract the three types of secondary afflictions (upakleśa) respectively.
The three types of secondary affliction are:
failing to act toward beings who are equal, and failing to honor those who are superior.
He explains this threefold envy as follows: "envy toward equals" refers to envy toward those who have caused harm;
as its opposite, he says, "without rivals."
Hatred toward those who are inferior, harmful, or even helpful is that by which one would afflict those beings.
As an antidote to this, he says: "without malice" (*avyāpanna*).
It is called "vast" (*vipula*) because it is vast due to its great undertaking (*mahāprasthāna*), applying the name of the effect to the cause, or because its object is vast; thus they recite "vast."
The dyad consisting of the stationary and the moving; the dyad of all things, whether insentient or sentient;
[154] and the immeasurable, due to the vastness of the bases for the beings of the desire realm who possess limitless desires.
Beyond five hundred and twenty [miles], there is a return;
for the object is indeed a tiger or the like. That very thing, as a result, is the echo. What is illuminated by this, which begins most abundantly on all sides and is pure?
"One [is] two-fold in form.
By means of the container, that which is contained within it is indicated, just as in the expression: "The lamps, together with their vessels, shine brightly."

"Facing toward" (*abhimukhya*) indicates the mental applications (*manaskāra*) directed toward that goal. The "briny waters" are the Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*), and the "state of joy" is mental gladness (*muditībhāva*). They "dwell" (*viharaṃti*) because they function through the fivefold attainment (*samāpatti*). As it has been stated for the first, so it should be understood for the second and subsequent ones; thus he says: "likewise by the second and the others. "The world completely withdrawn" refers to its state of being subject to desire, because it takes as its object sentient beings belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).
Having shown that this objection is established by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), he says: "In this way, by the inability to withstand conceptual construction," and so forth.

Concluding the explanation, he says: "These are the four divine abodes (*brāhmavihāra*). It is called "divine" (*brāhma*) because of its greatness; for the cultivation of loving-kindness and the others yields a great fruit. Therefore, they are called the "divine abodes. And these immeasurables, beginning with loving-kindness, are called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) because their objects are immeasurable. For what purpose are they fourfold? [They are] for the sake of counteracting, respectively, ill-will (*vyāpāda*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and sensual passion (*kāmarāga*).
In that regard, for those with an abundance of ill will, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the antidote for its abandonment;

for those with an abundance of harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), compassion (*karuṇā*) is the antidote for its abandonment; and for those with an abundance of discontent (*arati*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is the antidote for its abandonment.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is for the purpose of abandoning those who abound in sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
What is the distinction between favoring (*anugraha*) and equanimity within the antidote to sensual desire?
Favoring is the cultivation of sexual passion, whereas equanimity is the [cultivation] of passion for one's mother, father, children, or wife.
Such is the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of loving-kindness and the others:
by attending to the thought, "O, may sentient beings be happy," one attains loving-kindness;
by attending to the thought, "O, sentient beings are suffering," one attains compassion.

One cultivates sympathetic joy (*muditā*) by attending to the thought, "May beings indeed rejoice! But by attending to "beings" alone, one attains equanimity (*upekṣā*), due to its neutrality. [117] How does a beginner produce compassion?

Just as one perceives oneself or hears of others who are suffering, being impelled by the inspiration of the Buddha's teaching, so too one directs one's mind toward the happiness of all, thinking: "Alas, may all beings be thus free from suffering!"

And one does not desire [this] for anyone; rather, because of the emergence of sentient beings, one directs that happiness toward the side of friends, then toward neutral persons, then toward enemies, and then toward friends who were previously enemies.
From there, one proceeds to the middle group, and then to those whom one hates.
Among these, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is cultivated; therein, the side of neutral persons is [regarded as] neither friend nor enemy.
Then, having abandoned that happiness toward the enemy's side, toward friends, and toward enemies, one becomes joyful;
then toward neutral parties, and then toward enemies. In that regard, "toward enemies" means toward those who are hostile, and "toward the side of friends" means a desire for them.

Just as the mental orientation toward happiness proceeds, from that [orientation] compassion arises; from the entire supreme *sāmbhogika*-kāya, the whole universe flashes forth, and as far as all the worlds, it flashes forth through loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

By seeing only the qualities in every object, he quickly generates loving-kindness; even in the case of a *pratyekabuddha*, who might otherwise perceive faults, it occurs solely by seeing the fruits of former merit.
When one applies such reflection, thinking: "These beings are engaged in practices fraught with many obstacles;

they are characterized by suffering and extreme suffering," it is by this very method that one is established [in compassion], thinking: "May these beings be faced with [the presence of] me. Equanimity, however, is realized through the perception of neutrality. [11]
Four paths of practice have been taught. To explain them, he says:
"Therein, in sequence," and so forth.
The difficult path of practice is that which is to be known through the sixth supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).

In the path of the fourth [dhyāna] when one has ascended to the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the [higher] formless realms, the practice is difficult (*duḥkhā pratipad*). It is called a "difficult practice" because it proceeds with effort; for while there is no grasping of the senses and no desire for practice, it nevertheless requires exertion. Furthermore, due to the application of tranquility (*śamatha*) and the absence of grasping, it proceeds with effort in the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna, and the formless realms.
In practices such as the handling of glowing coals, because they require effort due to the lack of mastery, they involve exertion;
therefore, on the path of the Anāgamya and other stages, it is a difficult practice.
This noble practice of the sixth supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) is what is known as the "sixth supernormal knowledge."
The meaning of "sixth" is the sense-object of the ear;
or alternatively, it refers to that which is to be known by the sixth person—the meaning of the mind as the sense-object of the ear. [200]
He says "iḍgiḍakaraṇe" in order to explain this very point in detail:
"by nature" means by its own inherent character;
it occurs when there is an intense accumulation [of merit].
For whoever is characterized by an excessive temperament of passion is said to be such when passion arises for them even at the slightest object;
likewise for those with intense hatred and intense delusion. Therefore, it is in this way that their activity proceeds.
His creation was a marvel;
these five— faith and the others—
are the supramundane ornaments.
Regarding "the sixfold path" (*ṣaḍvidhā pratipat*): there are six paths.
Therein, "the path of swift intuition" (*kṣiprābhijñā*) refers to the path of suffering (*duḥkhā*), as previously explained.
The path in which there is higher knowledge through wisdom is itself "higher knowledge through wisdom" (*dhiyābhijñā*). This refers to those of sharp, middling, and other faculties.
Alternatively, *dhiṣaṇya* means the marvelous higher knowledge arising from the mind; that itself is "higher knowledge through wisdom."
The path is sharp and swift;
the remainder is as before.
(3) In that regard, what is the pleasant practice with quick higher knowledge?
In the second, third, and fourth stages (*bhūmi*) among the [remaining] nine stages, the path is called "the easy practice" (*sukhā pratipad*),
because it is free from effort due to the absence of cause, right seclusion, perception, and exertion.
"With higher knowledge" (*dhanyābhijñā*) is as explained previously.
(4) In that regard, what is the pleasant practice characterized by higher knowledge? It is as before:
it is the "uninterrupted concentration" (*ānantarya-samādhi*), by which the non-momentary state on the Mahāyāna path is grasped by the great lords. [116]
The cultivation of concentration through equanimity has been explained according to the practice.
Pointing this out, he says: "In that regard, monks, what is the cultivation of concentration free from outflows?
It is when practiced," and so forth.
Therein, it is cultivated through the cultivation of repeated practice;
it is developed through the abandonment of opposing factors;
and it is made abundant through the distancing from sense objects.
Alternatively, they have been practiced during the stage of the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*),
cultivated during the stage of the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*),
and repeatedly performed with all their primary and secondary components. To demonstrate how these lead to the attainment of meditative equipoise in due order, he says "therein," and so forth.
By these phrases beginning with "having gone for refuge," he demonstrates physical withdrawal (*kāyavyapakarṣa*).

One who dwells without a companion becomes physically withdrawn by virtue of distancing oneself from the company of people. "He contemplates according to reality" means that he observes with wisdom in accordance with the days free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
By the words "hairy" (*romaṇvat*) and so forth, he demonstrates its attractiveness, because it removes unwholesome [qualities] through discernment.
*Śiroruhāḥ* means hair; *rambhu* means the loss of threads, and *romāṇi* means body hairs. It is "wounded on both sides."
In the Middle Country, it is commonly understood that "a storehouse for rice" refers to a granary for mung beans;
thus, "for the grasping of passion" means it serves to grasp the passion of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*).
Because the teaching bears its fruit merely by the resolution of what is to be done.
(2) Showing the second cultivation, he says: "for dwelling in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihārāya*).
"The present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma*) refers to the object [of experience] in the present birth. A "dwelling" (*vihāra*) that is pleasant is "dwelling in happiness" (*sukhavihāra*).

"Abiding in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharme sukhavihāra*) means for the sake of that abiding in happiness in the present life. The word *dṛṣṭa* (seen) refers to what is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*). By the word *dharma*, birth (*janma*) is also meant. This is what is intended: one should practice the bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi-sukha*) in this very birth; such is the meaning.
"This very body, detached from [sensual desires] and born of seclusion," and so forth—what is "born of seclusion"? It is joy and bliss (*prīti-sukha*). What, then, is this so-called "seclusion"?

In the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), there arises the sevenfold quality beginning with "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Through these distinctions, a gradual and gentle excellence in the nourishment of the body and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is described.

This body, composed of the four elements, has the form of everything from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head; it is sustained for the sake of the self by earth and the other elements. Just as the fruits of the *nyagrodha* tree and others are sustained internally and externally by the moisture of water, so too the body, sustained by all that is watery, occupies a certain region within the wheel of the bodily locations. And this cultivation of dwelling in happiness in the present life is to be understood as the cultivation belonging specifically to those who have attained the first dhyāna and the others. By this, all other meditations (*dhyāna*) are included. [205]

Meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) by means of the instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth does not pertain to those whose faces are turned toward the future life (*saṃparāya-mukha*). This is because for non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who have entered the first dhyāna, as well as for those following the first dhyāna, there is an absence of being "facing the future life.

Furthermore, it is inappropriate for those with great pride (*mahogha*) and for those following what is unwholesome (*ayuktānugata*), because when they attain that meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), there is an absence of being "facing the future life."
(3) To demonstrate the third [type], he says: "Knowledge-vision" (*jñānadarśana*) and so forth.
Knowledge itself is vision; thus it is "knowledge-vision," which is a minute portion of the first increase. Even a minute portion of the first increase is designated as "vision."

That very cognition, being the first increase, is intended to be called "vision" (*darśana*). Its preparatory application (*prayoga*) consists of the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) preceded by the ideation of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*). Therefore, he says: "the ideation of light," and so forth.

As long as the object of the range [of meditation] is well-grasped through vision, so long will cultivation reach completion even while walking. Therefore, he explains the application [of the mind] so that one is not released from the range: "The perception of light is maintained until it is well-grasped.
At the time of the range, because it is withdrawn and free from fear, it is well-grasped.
Because it is grasped with right view at the time of reflection and because of the application of mental clarity, it is well-grasped;

because of the application of the arising of excellence at the time of cultivation, it is well-seen; and because of the application of accomplishment regarding well-refined objects, it is well-mastered knowledge. [206]
The "perception of evenness" means the perception of light. Regarding the phrase "together with radiance":

that yogi cultivates the mind together with radiance, which is to say, with light. How so? It says: "as by day, so by night. This is the "perception of the world" in all its states; because it proceeds through the stages of cultivation, the entire world is suffused with light.
It pervades. In the state of being pervaded, darkness has departed.
He speaks of the fourth cultivation: "the attainment of wisdom.
The attainment of wisdom is *prajñāpratilambha*; it is said for that purpose. It is for the sake of obtaining a distinction in wisdom, for the sake of obtaining the excellence of wisdom.

Or rather, demonstrating that, he says: "In that regard, the cultivation of meditative concentration (samādhi-bhāvanā) is to be performed until one dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna. Why is it that through the cultivation of the fourth dhyāna there is the attainment of wisdom (prajñā)? It is said:

because the fourth dhyāna here consists of eighteen modes, and thus serves as the basis for all the qualities of the yogis' mental resolves (saṃkalpa). And those qualities are specific forms of wisdom (prajñā-viśeṣa).
There are four cultivations of concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā*).
[The suffix] *-bhāvanā* may indeed be understood as expressing the act of cultivation itself, even when it does not specify a particular object.
Immediately after the cultivation of concentration, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are explained.
He says this regarding them: "In that regard, monks, why are there four foundations of mindfulness?
Here, the four are the foundations of mindfulness of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
Why are there exactly four, neither fewer nor more?"

Because of the fourfold secondary afflictions and their opposites, the four foundations of mindfulness are taught as their respective antidotes; for the antidotes to the various types of secondary afflictions are stated in sequence. Among them, the foundation of mindfulness regarding the body is described here: "In this case, monks, a monk... [209] ...in the internal treasury, observing the body in the proximate body. "Observing" refers to wisdom.

That person who observes reality as it is is like a staff; thus, he is one who observes the body in the body, having transcended past forms. By means of equanimity regarding specific and general characteristics, he is "ardent," meaning possessed of vigor. He is "mindful," meaning one whose faculties are governed by mindfulness. "Walking with clear comprehension" means being endowed with wisdom. Having subdued...
"In the world, covetousness and dejection [are abandoned]. Alternatively, this has the sense of "freedom from passion.

Why is the subduing of covetousness and dejection mentioned, rather than that of all afflictions? It is said: the term "all" should be understood here in the sense of "proximity. Or else, by the subduing of covetousness, the subduing of bodily desire is expressed.

Through the subduing of mental distress (*daurmanasya*), there is the subduing of ill-will (*vyāpāda*). Through ardent effort and mindfulness, there is the subduing of sloth and torpor (*styānamiddha*). Through being mindful, there is the subduing of restlessness and regret (*auddhatyakaukṛtya*). Through acting with clear comprehension (*saṃprajānacārī*), there is the subduing of doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Thus, for one whose hindrances (*nivaraṇa*) have been suppressed, the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) consists in the contemplation of the body in the body. By this, the impossibility of future existence [is realized].
The support for the body has been shown.
To express the continuum of others, he says: "externally, by means of the effect," and so forth.
Demonstrating the expression of both continuums, he says: "internally and externally," and so forth.
Now, what is the intention behind the abandonment of both the internal and the external? It is said:
[the Buddha] teaches the defilements (*kleśa*) as a single cognition both internally and externally, not as a single cognition through a teaching of non-differentiation;
for in both cases, they do not exist as [intrinsic] pleasure.
Now, what is the meaning of "body" (kāya)? It means an aggregate (saṃghāta).
Now, regarding the phrase "contemplating the body in the body," this refers to the second [meaning]. What is the intended meaning? That is explained as follows:
For one who contemplates the investigation of feelings within the body, [the perceptions] become non-perverted.

However, regarding the body, it is for the sake of vision that one is said to be "one who sees the body as the body," according to what has been taught. Likewise, even in the case of the application of mindfulness to the investigation of feelings, because mindfulness is distinct from the self, there is a threefold division. The applications of mindfulness have the nature of wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. 2.
Why is wisdom called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)? It is said:

because mindfulness is established through wisdom regarding the body and so forth, just as one calls it "recollection" from the act of recollecting; therefore, wisdom is the foundation of mindfulness.
Having the body as its object, internally, with a continuous flow, one dwells contemplating the body in the body, observing the body.
By means of that [mindfulness], the contemplation of that [body] proceeds through inhalations and exhalations.
How so? Because there exists for one who contemplates objects with dependence.
What is that duality? It is said: [the body and the breath].
The characteristic of vision is the observation of duality;
however, the subsequent non-observation is like [the perception of] a staff.
Therefore, it is the observation of the non-existent.
"One who contemplates the body is a 'contemplator of the body' (kāyānupaśyanī).

This means that because contemplating the body is his play (*līlā*), he is a "contemplator of the body. Just as one who desires to drink succeeds in drinking, so too does this succeed for him; such is the meaning of the verse.

[312] Wisdom is not the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) up to the knowledge of the stages (*bhūmijñatā*); wisdom is likewise not [the application of mindfulness] in the applications of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
In this way, there is an examination of the body and so forth by means of wisdom that discerns their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and other characteristics (*anyalakṣaṇa*).
Among these, the own characteristic—the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—of the body is as described in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.
For feeling, it is the state of experiencing (*anubhavatva*).
Regarding the objects of focus for the mind and consciousness:
among the phenomena that constitute the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*),
their respective intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are as follows.
Their general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), however, is impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness.
Regarding the statement that mindfulness is "purified through association," he says: [it concerns] things as they have been seen, heard, or experienced.

What is the sequence designated by desire and so forth? The application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*); what is the sequence for the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)?

It is said: Action is as previously described. Why is there liberation from action? Because each respective [application of mindfulness] was previously seen. Or rather, because of the non-abiding of sensual desire within the body, and because that [desire] is not perceived by the mind. That is the non-perception of the mind’s initial movement, due to the abandonment of its lack of mastery. Their names are indeed in this very order: for instance, the body is the object of the application of mindfulness of the body;
the same should be applied to feeling and the others. Thus, the applications of mindfulness have been explained. [214]

Immediately following that, the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are explained. As it is said: "In that regard, what are the four right efforts? They are called 'right efforts' because they are efforts for the sake of purification, or because they are primary efforts. [The text continues:

"Regarding the detailed explanation of the 'abandonment of unwholesome states,' this refers to the arising, association, and improper placement of unwholesome states such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
By means of bringing under control the conduct that is the basis for the removal of wisdom, one generates desire (*chanda*)."

For in the passage beginning with "desire is long-suffering," the mention of laziness (*kausīdya*) is intended to show that one must abandon those [hindrances]; it indicates that desire is the root [of diligence]. Regarding "calm" (*śamatha*), it refers to the Mahāyāna which leads to darkness; because one does not quickly grasp it, it is explained as being like a barren field. And for this twofold grasping, one initiates vigor (*vīrya*) through frequent practice (*bahulīkāra*). In that context, "frequent practice" consists of continuous action.

This is the aspect of *idā*. Having performed the preparatory action (*saṃskṛtya*), one impels the mind that contemplates dissolution (*layabhāvanā*) through a concentrated mind, and causes the mind that contemplates zeal (*autsukyabhāvanā*) to enter.

One recollects them. Of whom? Of those very reciters (*pāṭaka*), who are striving with a mind of intense devotion through constant recollection and mindfulness. "One generates desire" is as explained before. Likewise, one recollects the wholesome qualities (*kuśala*).

In the *Nānāmahṛdaya*: "Zeal (*chanda*)" is as explained previously. For those very wholesome qualities such as faith (*śraddhā*) that are being recollected, one generates zeal for their cultivation; this is as explained previously. Alternatively, it means that one generates zeal through the application arising from the "head" (*śīrṣaprayoga*). This refers to the gateway of application.
He explains: A certain [bodhisattva], such as Maitreya, Sakumārī, or Udāyin, initiates vigor from the moment of becoming a bodhisattva;
by the power of one-pointed tranquility (*śamatha*), he calms the mind, and by the power of one-pointed insight (*vipaśyanā*), he directs the mind.
These two, in turn, arise sequentially like the rising of moonlight.
Having moved along the path on the earth, he states the application:
"Generate desire. This means that through the investigation of the body, one brings the body and the mind face-to-face.

By the excellence of the moonlight-like garden, one protects vigor. How does one protect it? One stretches out the withered mind by means of the moisture of the objects of desire, which are like the marks of a fresh wound.
Having uplifted the mind, one should properly grasp it for oneself;

this means that one maintains and sets it in motion. Likewise, there is the non-decline of wholesome states that have arisen, which is their stability; there is the increase of enthusiasm, which is their further development; and there is the absence of discouragement, which is their fulfillment.
This is the equanimity regarding the sixfold group of human goals.
The battle of the gazelle and the path—these two have shown the fourfold goal.
Thus, it should be understood that these are the complete preliminary practices (*pūrvāṅga*) for the transition into the path (*vīthī-saṅkrānti*).
Now, why was either the chain (*śṛṅkhalana*) or the wing of the drum (*druṇapakṣa*) presented first?
It is said:
For a superior point is easily understood when it follows a sequence;
indeed, the dark fortnight or traveling to a foreign land is easily comprehended [only in that order]. [116]
Immediately after the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) are the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda).
Showing these, he says: "In that regard, there are successively the four bases of psychic power.
Psychic power (*ṛddhi*) is the accomplishment (*samṛddhi*) of all qualities, beginning with the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).

The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are the feet because they are the foundation of that psychic power; the meaning is that they are the means for attaining psychic power. Furthermore, these are characterized by investigation through the path of the eight formative applications (*saṃskāra*). Showing them in their proper order, he says:
In this context, monks, "a monk [possesses] the concentration of zeal and the exertions," and so forth.
Concentration caused by zeal is "concentration of zeal. The meaning is that it occurs in successive order, with zeal as the predominant factor.

In this context, *chandasamādhi* (concentration through desire) is that by which, through the elimination of the obstacles such as lack of mastery (*adhipatya*) and so forth, one touches upon the state of mental readiness (*cittakāmatā*). The "formative effort for abandonment" (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) refers to the volitional effort for the sake of abandonment. For what purpose is it for abandonment? It is for the abandonment of the five faults: laziness (*kausīdya*), lack of faith (*samaya*), excitement (*auddhatya*), lack of disillusionment (*anirveda*), and being distracted by worldly concerns (*saṃkīrṇa*). Furthermore, the formative effort for abandonment is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*) by means of the characteristics of: reliance on the non-forgetting of desire (*chanda*), exertion (*vyāyāma*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), clear comprehension (*samprajanya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). This is the formative effort for the cultivation of concentration through desire.
"One cultivates the basis of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) that is endowed with, accompanied by, and joined to those two" refers to cultivation through determination (*niyamanabhāvanā*).
"Dependent on seclusion" (*vivekaniśrita*): that by which the unwholesome (*akuśala*) is distinguished away—that is, abandoned—is "seclusion" (*viveka*); it refers to the Path (*mārga*).
That which is based on that, following its sequence; or, that which takes recourse in that.
"Based on dispassion" means:
The abandonment of passion is dispassion; this is the meaning of "nirvāṇa.
Regarding the phrase "dependent on cessation":
for the disciple, however, cessation is dissociation.
That is its basis. Regarding "transformed by relinquishment" (*vyavasargopariṇata*):
in the sense of exclusion, that conditioned thing is abandoned within affliction; since that [abandonment] exists, it is "relinquishment," which is disjunction (*visaṃyoga*). [222]

The meaning is that it is conducive to that. (2) He states the second: "energy-concentration" (*vīrya-samādhi*), and so forth. In this context, energy-concentration is when, having taken up the burden of awakening through continuous application, the one-pointedness of the mind flashes forth. The rest is as before. (3) He states the third: "mind-concentration" (*citta-samādhi*), and so forth. Mind-concentration is when, having grasped the energy of the previous concentration, one flashes forth the one-pointedness of the mind while maintaining this very mind. The rest is as before.

(4) He states the fourth: "the concentration of investigation" (*mīmāṃsā-samādhi*). Investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). That concentration of investigation is the one-pointedness of mind which flashes forth while discerning its object. The remainder is as before; thus, it is said that these are the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) consisting of concentration. [16] Immediately after the bases of psychic power, the monk’s meritorious qualities are mentioned. They are precisely those: the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) cultivated therein.
Namely: the faculty of faith up to the faculty of wisdom.
Faith is clarity of mind;
it is the longing for and the aspiration toward wholesome dharmas.
Mindfulness is the restraint of the underlying tendencies;
concentration is one-pointedness of mind; wisdom is the discernment of phenomena. [224]
Furthermore, regarding the sequence of the faculties:
one who is not yet a śramaṇa but seeks the fruit applies himself to awakening;
however, due to laziness and aversion, his mindfulness is lost.
One whose mindfulness is established attains concentration characterized by specific qualities.
With a concentrated mind, one understands things as they have arisen:
namely, those belonging to the realm of saṃsāra.
"Belonging to the sphere of saṃsāra. "Worldly":
that which exists in the world (loka) is worldly; such [is it].
O one of right view, for the sake of thoroughly protecting against the next world:
"kalyāṇam" means wholesome;
"paudgalam" means unwholesome.
I shall experience the ripening of mixed unwholesome and wholesome [karma].
Supported by awakening and mindfulness, may there be no lack of enthusiasm for wholesome deeds, and through the non-manifestation [of faults], may I awaken.
Through the remainder, one does not incur defects; one should desire the life-force that seeks the non-perception of objective supports.
One performs it repeatedly; one applies oneself with clarity to a single-pointed mental object.
One realizes—that is, one directly perceives—each respective sphere, because the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) consists in the discernment of phenomena (*dharmavicaya*).
[116] He states that the other faculty is power: "The five powers are the same as the faculties."
"Endowed with faith," and so forth,
up to "endowed with wisdom.
These same five faculties, beginning with faith, are called powers when they become powers.

And how is their power to be described? Because they are not overcome by their opposites—lack of faith and so forth—which cause one to turn away from the object of liberation and lead to conduct inconsistent with them; therefore, they are called "powers. Furthermore, the faculties (*indriya*) are the opposites of those [powers]. The nature of reality is experienced through the manifestation of these five.
The state of being double [in strength] is said to result from having completely conquered the moments of poison and so forth;
thus, the powers (balas) are explained.
Those very factors are called the limbs of enlightenment (bodhyaṅgas).
From the explanation of these, [it follows that] "the others" and so forth refer here to the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
He says: from the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness up to equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding the term "factor of enlightenment" (*saṃbodhyaṅga*): what, then, is enlightenment here, and what is a factor of enlightenment? It is said:
[it is] through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
And for the sake of the meaning beginning with "awakening" (*bodhi*):
the limbs of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) themselves are the "expanses" (*viśāni*). In that context, "awakening" (*saṃbodha*) refers to that in which there is awakening.
And that person remains as such until the awakening of a Pratyekabuddha;

[the awakening of] one who has attained the realization of the momentary truth through the faculty of noble patience is called "awakening" because its essence consists in the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
And because they act as companions to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it is unshakable.
Furthermore, mindfulness and the others are the six factors that serve as the means to awakening (*bodhi*). Among them, mindfulness [is the factor] for awakening—[230]

The "grasping of the heap" (*rāśigrāha*) is [the basis for the designation of a person], because it is through the similarity of that [heap] to a support (*āśraya*) that there is no distinction [between them].

Investigation (*vicaya*) is the limb of the basis of dharma (*dharmasthabhāva*), because both knowledge and the basis of dharma exist within awakening. Energy (*vīrya*) is the limb of departure (*niryāṇāṅga*), because by means of it one proceeds toward the transcendence of the mass of suffering. Joy (*prīti*) is the limb of happiness (*sukhāṅga*), because it is the cause of physical and mental well-being. Tranquility (*praśrabdhi*)—[is the limb of concentration...]*

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is a factor of non-affliction, because it serves as the antidote to those afflictions. Furthermore, it is equanimity regarding mental formations (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*), not equanimity regarding feeling (*vedanā-upekṣā*), because of the mention of "joy" (*prīti*); for joy has the nature of mental pleasure (*saumanasya*). Moreover, even in a single moment of consciousness, it is impossible for there to be the cessation of the disturbances caused by feeling and so forth; therefore, since it is that [equanimity] which pertains to mental formations, it is called the "factor of equanimity."

The path of cultivation, characterized by the factors of enlightenment, is called the "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*). It is said that these are the limbs of vigor. Immediately after the factors of enlightenment, the factors of the path are explained. He states them: "In that regard, what is the noble eightfold path?
He replies: "Right view, up to right concentration."
In this context, the noble path factors beginning with right view are established in their respective order as the antidotes to wrong view and so forth, up to the antidote to wrong concentration.
Furthermore, for one who has entered the noble path, all eight path factors exist simultaneously in a single moment.
Let it be granted that these factors, such as right view and the rest, exist.
How do right speech, right action, and right livelihood exist for one who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpanna*)?
Does he cultivate something external by their power, or does he perform some [external act], or does he see robes and so forth? Certainly not.
How, then, are they established as being present by their power? It is said:

One attains this by possessing a mind that has entered into that path. Alternatively: having emerged from that attainment, one proceeds toward those [states] that are not subject to deliberation (*asaṃpradhārgāmiṣu*), but one does not proceed toward those states that remain subject to deliberation. Others, having applied the term "anger" (*kopa*) without distinction, accuse [the practitioner]; in that case, what is to be done with such a person?

Furthermore, according to the Sautrāntikas, through the non-conceptual awakening (*nirnimittābhisambodhi*) of the path and its meditative attainments, the practitioner obtains the designation of the "path that is not lost" (*anuluptamārga*) regarding the ultimate path (*arthamārga*).
By virtue of obtaining this, even though [the manifest path] has ceased, it does not proceed again toward rebirth in the lower realms (*apāya*) and so forth;
rather, it proceeds toward association with the noble ones (*saṃprayoga*) and the attainment of the higher stages.
Therefore, by way of the metaphorical designation of cause and effect, all eight path-factors are established;
however, they do not exist as such in their own intrinsic nature. Thus, mindfulness of breathing has sixteen aspects.
Those winds which enter are "in-breaths" (ānāḥ);
those winds which are expelled are "out-breaths" (apānāḥ).
The mindfulness that follows both of these is "mindfulness of breathing" (ānāpānasmṛti).
This very wisdom has mindfulness as its object.
However, the mention of "mindfulness" (smṛti) is an indication of both mindfulness and feeling (vedanā) regarding the nature of wisdom.
Furthermore, in that regard, when the yogi has fully mastered mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (ānāpānasmṛti):
One must rely upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), because the teaching on cultivation (*bhāvanāvāda*) is purified by that.
Likewise, one must possess pure ethical discipline (*viśuddhaśīla*), be endowed with hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*), and avoid being distracted by worldly affairs.
For it is in this way that that cultivation is perfected, and not otherwise.
He points these out here with the words "the sixteen aspects" (*ṣoḍaśākārān*) beginning with "breathing in" (*bhinnuḥ*).
"Clearly breathing in, I clearly breathe in"—he understands this according to its actual occurrence.

"Clearly breathing out, I clearly breathe out"—he understands this according to its actual occurrence. Such is the form [of the first aspect], because it is a general observation of all the constituent parts.
The remaining explanation of this [term] consists of its specific aspects characterized by long, short, and so forth, because it takes on the form of observing particular features.

In that context, "clear" (*sphuṭa*) means extremely distinct. "He understands" (*prajānāti*) refers to the progress of one who has engaged in that very cultivation through the power of repeated practice; thus, [the breath] becomes fully manifest. (1) "Breathing in long," and so forth—this means "long" in terms of duration.
(2) Regarding "therein, the short [vowel]": the movement of internal wisdom (*ādhyātma-prajñā*) is observed as it discerns.

(3) And "penetrating all bodily formations" (*sarvakāya-saṃskāra-prativedhya*): all those bodily formations are what is manifested; they belong to internal wisdom. One whose nature is the realization of reality (*tattvika-saṃvedana*) through application to that [wisdom], perceives that these are merely designations for the entire body (*sarvakāya-prajñapti*). (4) And "penetrating joy" (*prīti-prativedhya*): the experience of joy [is found] in the first and second dhyānas.
And because of the experience of mental well-being (*saumanasya*), there is equanimity (*sāma*). Joy (*prīti*) is designated as mental well-being.
One who experiences "dryness" (*śuṣka*) is a trace (*leśa*). It would be logical that one entering the first and second dhyānas experiences that dryness;
however, in the attainment of the third dhyāna, the mind is dry. [This concerns] equanimity and bliss (*upekṣā-sukha*).
Regarding the praise of being without food and without breath, how can one be said to "breathe in while experiencing joy and bliss"? It is replied:

this is not a fault. One who breathes in while seeking joy and pure joy-bliss directed toward external objects is called "one who experiences it subtly. In that case, would it not follow that the intention is "one should not withdraw oneself [from the world]"?
