It may be so. However, it is precisely the destruction of the self that is the basis of application; or rather, because [the self] is grasped through the destruction of its own basis.

(6) The sign of the bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*) is being calmed. Through tranquility, while being calmed, one leads it to attenuation during entry, thereby abandoning it. This attenuation is the third stage of abandonment, due to the casting off of the hindrances. In this abandonment—
From the fourth dhyāna, having been released from all sides by the light [of the signless],
he is one who experiences the mental aspect of the signless. This means he is characterized by the experience of the mental formations of the mind,
having attained the meditative absorptions and attainments according to his own disposition, wherein perception and feeling have ceased.

(8) Or, [one enters] the state of fear regarding the danger of being pierced by the agitation of the mind. Desiring the impact of a hard heart upon the subtle space, one should abandon all that gives rise to conflict.

(9) Regarding "penetrating the mind": one should penetrate the pure mind through the power of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of awakening; one should dispel the cognition that has verbal objects as its support through the application of the fourth dhyāna attainment.

(10) "Gladdening" (*abhipramodayan*) means from the removal of the three types of dejection (*daurmanasya*). One "joins with the seal" (*mudrā*) is what is meant by "gladdening. For it is thus: through association with sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha*), [the mind] becomes sluggish; through association with restlessness (*auddhatya*), it becomes weak or middling. Thus, those freed from such unevenness are called "unified" (*ruṇḍā*); therefore, it is termed "gladdening. This is because one withdraws certain signs (*nimitta*) that have not yet been fully extended. Or, having experienced that which is accompanied by purity (*śuddhatā-sahagata*), it is termed "gladdening."
(11) He concentrated his mind, directing it toward the aspect of the Teacher within meditative absorption; experiencing that which was previously associated with the Teacher,
(12) he thought, "I am being liberated," because of the removal of the obstacles to higher meditative absorption,
or because of the liberation from the field of existence.

(13) "One who contemplates impermanence in the impermanent" means one who perceives impermanence in that which is sought after as being impermanent; that is, regarding the objects of desire or all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). (14) "One who contemplates dispassion" means one who perceives that even within the lightning-like [objects], there is an absence of passion (*rāga*).
Dispassion; the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); one who contemplates that;

"one who contemplates cessation" (*nirodhānudarśin*). Cessation is the natural stopping of all afflictions (*kleśa*); it is merely the state of having fallen away from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). One who contemplates that.
(16) "Contemplating relinquishment" means: relinquishment is through the act of relinquishing;
it is the laying down of the burden of the aggregates that has extended from beginningless time. One trains oneself by contemplating that, thinking: "I shall relinquish the basis.

Others, however, say: "Whether long or short, it is the breath of the Śākyas. Due to the proximity of the sequence of application, it is long when it possesses power; and it is short when it has returned to its natural state. This demonstrates the degree of sharpness or dullness of one's wisdom. For the beginner, the observation becomes very clear as they abide in a state of non-separation from the meditative concentration (*akṣāsamādhāna*). Because of this clarity, they desire intense abandonment. At that time, the yogin should practice with lengthening until the sign (*nimitta*) is perceived. Once the sign is established, one should remain exactly as before. This is the essential point here: "long" is as previously described. And herein, wherever the support for the inhalation and exhalation is not excessive, there the inhalation [is measured] by twenty finger-breadths within the nose.
The methods for the practice of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) are described as the "stages ending with the mastery of the lamp" (*dīpeśāparaparyanta*).

He states them: "In that regard, what are the stages ending with the mastery of the lamp? They are eight: the stage of the mastery of the lamp, the stage of the shaking of the lamp, the stage of the knowing of the lamp, and the stage of the continuity of the cause."
And these [qualities] consist of unwavering confidence in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as bodily knowledge and the non-lapse of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
He states them in sequence: (1) "Through unwavering confidence in the Buddha," and so forth.

All phenomena beginning with the Buddha’s teaching are the Buddha; he is called the Buddha because he has brought about the qualities of a Buddha. Confidence in these is the state of the mind being free from the impurity (*rajas*) of passion and the like.
[241] Regarding the Buddha, there is serene confidence (*prasāda*) through the destruction of power (*urjekṣaya*).

What is the meaning of "serene confidence through non-feeling" (*avedayaprasāda*)? It is the absence of association (*asaṃprayoga*) here with the perception of the truths as being otherwise than they are, as taught in the Sūtra. And that [absence] is established at the time of attaining the treatise (*śāstra*).
He explains it according to how one brings about its excellence, as in the detailed passage beginning, "Thus also is the Blessed One," and so forth.

By these terms, the greatness of its merit is described in due order: [1] discipline, [2] faith, [3] following the moon, [4] the examination of the nature of things, and [5] the reason why that Blessed One, having observed sentient beings as being either capable or incapable of liberation, disciplines those who are capable; and [6] how the truth is excellently established in this treatise. [242]

By the word "Bhagavān," he indicates that which is intended to be expressed; having considered the etymological derivation of "Bhagavān," it is indeed the Blessed One himself. What, then, is intended here as the complete collection of qualities constituting the status of a Teacher? It is the state of being a Buddha in this world. First, by means of his conduct, the complete collection of the status of a Teacher is distinguished: "The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One. Furthermore, he shows the complete collection of the status of a Teacher in another way.
And that collection of qualities constituting the state of being a Teacher is twofold: characterized by the quality of being a speaker and characterized by the quality of being a practitioner.

Being a speaker means being the author of unerring instruction, by which the Blessed One is called the Tathāgata; for by that very [quality], he grasps the Dharma without error. [The second consists of] the perfection of practice, the perfection of abandonment, and the perfection of knowledge.

In this context, the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the term *bhagavat* is stated as follows: he is called "Bhagavat" because he has slain his enemies (*ari-hata*). Here, "enemies" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), in the sense of being the source of fear and calamity for all afflictions.

He is said to be "perfectly awakened" (*samyaksambuddha*) by virtue of the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-sampad*), having awakened to the Dharma correctly and without error. Thus, he is called "Buddha" because he has awakened to enlightenment (*bodhi*).

To this extent, the treatise becomes perfectly complete—by virtue of teaching characteristics that are non-erroneous, by means of the knowledge of the entire collection of all that is to be known, and through the absence of delusion regarding all phenomena.
And this [perfection] is found only in the Blessed One.
Therefore, it is indicated that the Blessed One alone has attained the characteristic of a treatise in its entirety.
By the phrase "endowed with knowledge and conduct" (vidyācaraṇasampanna), he shows that this [teaching] possesses the characteristics of a scripture and serves as the cause for its attainment.
The path is most excellent through knowledge and conduct;
right view is knowledge.

Alternatively, its practice is twofold; or rather, one who has practiced both natures is not able to proceed—having said this, "knowledge and conduct" (*vidyācaraṇa*) refers to knowledge (*vidyā*) as the higher wisdom (*abhiprajñā*), and conduct (*caraṇa*) as the two trainings of higher ethics and higher concentration (*adhiśīla-samādhi*), because wisdom belongs to the preceding stage (*pūrvabhūmika*). Having said that conduct is what follows after [wisdom], it is called "conduct."

At the commencement of knowledge (*vidyā*), there is the instruction for those on the preceding stages regarding the purification of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

For it is by means of wisdom (*prajñā*) that the eye is truly produced; therefore, through ethical discipline and meditative concentration, one proceeds as if with feet and reaches what is to be reached.
Thus, by the term "knowledge and conduct" (*vidyācaraṇa*), the three trainings (*śikṣā*) are indicated.

By the term *sugata*, he shows that [the Buddha] has gone according to the knowledge of the treatises (*yathāśāstrajña*). He is *sugata* because he has gone to the unsurpassed state (*anuttaragatatva*) and because his afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) have been thoroughly destroyed.

The Sugata has gone without remainder, in the sense of having gone to the entirety of all that is to be known; he is the cause of the Sugatas. This fourfold nature is for the purpose of dispelling the views based on external things.
For those who have not previously understood [the truth] do not proceed according to their own whims.

Although the Āryakas and others have reached the state of *chanda*, they have not done so completely because of their lack of capacity, as they remain within the scope of further questioning; however, this is not due to a deficiency in knowledge regarding omniscience.

Thus, for the Blessed One—who has attained the perfection of mastery over the scriptures through the complete realization of the *vidyā-anuśāsana*—the *chanda* that seeks to behold his skill in knowing the scriptures reveals the meaning of the categories (*padārtha*) as the very source of the well-known objects of perception.
His quality of being a knower of the scriptures is twofold. [325]

as expressed in the passage beginning with "the world is manifold" and so forth,
